paths.name: Australia's Thermal and Metallurgical Coal Exports to Asia
origin_regions: Australia (Bowen Basin, Queensland; Hunter Valley, New South Wales)
chokepoints: Queensland and New South Wales rail-and-port export corridors (Port of Newcastle, Hay Point, Abbot Point, Gladstone)
Cyclone-season disruptions to Queensland coal ports and rail lines
Buyer concentration among a small number of Northeast and South Asian steelmakers and utilities
paths.why_it_matters: Australia is the world's second-largest coal exporter by volume and its largest exporter of metallurgical (coking) coal, the input steelmakers blend with iron ore in blast furnaces. Japan, China, India, and South Korea together take the large majority of Australian coal exports, so mine, rail, or port disruptions in Australia (frequent during the Queensland cyclone season) or shifts in Asian steel and power demand have an outsized effect on global seaborne coal prices, particularly for metallurgical coal.
historical_precedents: From October 2020, China halted customs clearance of Australian coal amid a broader trade dispute; Australian coal exports to China fell from several million tonnes a month to effectively zero through 2021, Australian thermal and metallurgical coal spot prices roughly doubled over the year as Chinese buyers turned to Indonesia, Russia, and Mongolia, and China itself experienced rolling domestic power shortages in September-October 2021; China resumed clearing some Australian coal cargoes in early 2023, per the International Energy Agency and industry reporting.
paths.estimated_global_share: Australia exported 363 million tonnes of coal in 2024 (about 25% of world coal exports by volume, second only to Indonesia), per the International Energy Agency's Coal 2025 report; Australia's metallurgical coal export volumes were projected to rise from 151 million tonnes in 2023-24 to 174 million tonnes by 2025-26, per Australia's Department of Industry, Science and Resources.

paths.name: Mongolia-China Coking Coal Corridor
origin_regions: Mongolia (South Gobi region: Tavan Tolgoi, Nariin Sukhait)
chokepoints: Gashuun Sukhait (Mongolia) - Ganqimaodu (China) border crossing
Tavan Tolgoi-Gashuun Sukhait dual-gauge railway (about 240 km)
Seasonal border-crossing capacity limits and, historically, cross-border health-control measures
destination_regions: China (Inner Mongolia, Hebei, and the broader national steel industry)
paths.why_it_matters: Mongolia has become China's largest source of imported coking coal, feeding blast furnaces in Hebei and other northern Chinese steelmaking hubs via a short overland route rather than seaborne shipping. Because most of this trade funnels through a single land border crossing and rail corridor, disruptions there, whether from border-capacity limits, infrastructure work, or cross-border health measures, can tighten coking coal supply for Chinese steelmakers even when seaborne coal keeps flowing from other exporters.
historical_precedents: Cross-border health-control measures between 2020 and early 2023 repeatedly slowed or halted truck crossings at Gashuun Sukhait-Ganqimaodu, at times cutting Mongolian coal exports to China well below pre-2020 levels; cross-border coal flows recovered only after Mongolia and China eased border restrictions in 2023, per industry trade reporting.

A dual-gauge rail line linking the Tavan Tolgoi mining complex in Mongolia to the Chinese rail network via Gashuun Sukhait-Ganqimaodu opened in September 2022, part of a buildout intended to raise cross-border rail capacity to an estimated 30-50 million tonnes a year and reduce reliance on truck transport, per Global Times and industry trade reporting.
paths.estimated_global_share: Mongolia shipped a new record 90.02 million tonnes of coal to world markets in 2025 (up 7.5% year over year from the prior record of 83.7 million tonnes in 2024), of which an estimated 75% was coking coal and roughly 90% went to China; Mongolia was China's largest single source of coking coal imports, ahead of Russia, per Mongolia's General Customs Department and Chinese customs data as reported by industry trade press (Mysteel).

paths.name: China's Domestic Coal Production and Power-Sector Demand
origin_regions: China (Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Inner Mongolia coal-mining provinces)
chokepoints: Domestic rail and highway coal-haulage corridors from Shanxi/Shaanxi/Inner Mongolia to coastal power-generating provinces
Mine-safety inspection regimes that can idle large shares of domestic mining capacity following accidents
Seasonal hydropower shortfalls that shift additional generation load onto coal-fired plants
destination_regions: China (national power grid and industrial users)
paths.why_it_matters: China produces and consumes more coal than any other country, using it to generate the majority of its electricity. Because China's coal market is overwhelmingly self-supplied rather than import-dependent, swings in Chinese domestic production, driven by mine-safety crackdowns, weather-linked hydropower shortfalls, or industrial demand surges, ripple into the smaller volume of coal China does import from world markets, moving global seaborne thermal coal prices even though most Chinese coal never crosses a border.
historical_precedents: In the second half of 2021, a combination of coal-mine-safety inspections, an anti-corruption campaign affecting mining in Inner Mongolia, and strong post-pandemic industrial demand tightened domestic coal supply; China experienced rolling power shortages across at least 18 of its 30 provincial-level regions in September-October 2021, with domestic spot coal prices roughly tripling from early-2021 levels, before the government eased production and pricing restrictions in response, per the International Energy Agency's Coal 2021 report.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for an estimated 58% of global coal consumption in 2024, consuming nearly 40% more coal than the rest of the world combined; China's electricity generation was 59.3% coal-fired in 2023, per the International Energy Agency's Global Energy Review 2025 and the U.S. Energy Information Administration's China Country Analysis Brief. More recently, fossil fuels (overwhelmingly coal) supplied about 58% of China's electricity in 2025, down from about 62% in 2024, with coal-fired generation falling year-on-year for the first time since 2015, per the energy think tank Ember.

paths.name: India's Coal-Fired Power Generation and Thermal Coal Imports
origin_regions: India (Coal India Limited fields in Jharkhand, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh)
chokepoints: Coal India Limited's near-monopoly on domestic production (roughly four-fifths of national output)
Rail capacity from inland coalfields to coastal power plants
East-coast import terminals (e.g. Paradip, Krishnapatnam, Mundra) receiving seaborne coal for blending
destination_regions: India (national power grid, supplemented for coastal and import-dependent plants by seaborne imports)
paths.why_it_matters: India is the world's second-largest coal consumer and coal-fired power generator, and coal supplies roughly 70% of its electricity. Although India produces most of the coal it burns, it still imports substantial volumes, chiefly from Indonesia, to blend with lower-quality domestic coal and to supply coastal plants far from domestic mines; a shortfall in either domestic output or import volumes can quickly threaten power-plant fuel stocks given India's fast-growing electricity demand and limited stockpile buffers.
historical_precedents: In October 2021, Indian coal stocks fell to critically low levels amid a global coal-price surge and a post-pandemic demand rebound; India's Central Electricity Authority reported that roughly 80% of monitored coal power plants held seven days' worth of coal or fewer, with about 30% down to one day or none, prompting several state governments to warn of imminent power shortages before supply stabilized, per India's Central Electricity Authority as reported by CNBC and other outlets.

paths.name: China's Dominance in Global Solar Panel Manufacturing
origin_regions: China (manufacturing base spanning Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Xinjiang, and other provinces)
chokepoints: Single-country manufacturing concentration exceeding 80% at every stage of production (polysilicon, ingots/wafers, cells, modules)
US and EU trade-remedy tariffs targeting Chinese-linked solar cells and modules
destination_regions: global utility-scale and rooftop solar markets
paths.why_it_matters: China's share of global manufacturing capacity exceeds 80% at every stage of the solar panel supply chain, from polysilicon through finished modules, a level of concentration the IEA has said is unmatched by any other major energy technology or fuel supply chain, including oil, gas, or coal. This gives Chinese industrial and trade policy outsized influence over global solar panel availability and pricing, and has repeatedly prompted the United States and European Union to pursue trade-defense measures and domestic manufacturing incentives aimed at diversifying supply.
historical_precedents: In October 2012, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed final antidumping duties of up to 249.96% and countervailing duties on Chinese-made crystalline silicon solar cells, following an October 2011 petition from SolarWorld and other U.S. manufacturers alleging underpriced Chinese imports were harming the domestic industry; the orders were later expanded to cover Taiwan-assembled cells in 2014.

Effective February 7, 2018, the United States imposed a Section 201 global safeguard tariff of 30% on imported crystalline-silicon solar cells and modules, with an annual duty-free exemption for the first 2.5 gigawatts of imported cells, stepping down five percentage points per year; the measure was extended by four years in 2022.
paths.estimated_global_share: China's share of global manufacturing capacity across polysilicon, ingots/wafers, cells, and modules exceeded 80% as of the IEA's 2022 Special Report on Solar PV Global Supply Chains, with polysilicon and wafer capacity on track to reach almost 95% by 2030 based on capacity under construction; Wood Mackenzie separately estimated China would hold more than 80% of global polysilicon, wafer, cell, and module manufacturing capacity every year from 2023 through 2026.

paths.name: Xinjiang Polysilicon Concentration in the Solar Supply Chain
chokepoints: Concentration of an estimated 40% of world polysilicon manufacturing in a single Chinese region (Xinjiang)
US forced-labor import compliance enforcement (Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act) affecting shipments with Xinjiang-linked material in their supply chain
paths.why_it_matters: Xinjiang alone accounts for an estimated 40% of the world's solar-grade polysilicon output, making a single Chinese region a foundational chokepoint for the entire downstream solar panel supply chain. Since the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act took effect on June 21, 2022, establishing a rebuttable presumption that goods made wholly or in part in Xinjiang are prohibited from U.S. entry, U.S. Customs and Border Protection has required importers to trace polysilicon provenance through multiple manufacturing tiers, adding compliance cost and shipment-detention risk that is distinct from ordinary trade-tariff exposure.
historical_precedents: The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act was signed into law on December 23, 2021 and took effect June 21, 2022, establishing a rebuttable presumption against the entry of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part in Xinjiang, per U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

From the law's effective date through early 2026, CBP detained an estimated $3.94 billion worth of shipments under UFLPA enforcement, of which about $3.26 billion fell under the electronics/solar-related product category, and multiple solar manufacturers (including Maxeon and Qcells-linked suppliers) publicly disclosed CBP detentions of panel or cell shipments in 2024-2025, per CBP enforcement statistics and company disclosures.
paths.estimated_global_share: Xinjiang accounted for an estimated 40% of global solar-grade polysilicon manufacturing, with China's polysilicon, ingot, and wafer production capacity overall on track to reach almost 95% of the world total by 2030, per the IEA's Special Report on Solar PV Global Supply Chains.

paths.name: Southeast Asia Solar Panel Assembly and Re-Export Route to the United States
chokepoints: Final-assembly operations in four Southeast Asian countries relying heavily on Chinese-made polysilicon, wafers, and cells
US antidumping/countervailing duty enforcement targeting circumvention of China-specific solar tariffs
paths.why_it_matters: After the United States imposed antidumping and countervailing duties on solar cells and modules from China starting in 2012, a large share of cell and module assembly capacity relocated to Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, which together supplied an estimated 84% of all U.S. solar cell and module imports in the fourth quarter of 2023. Because these Southeast Asian facilities remained heavily dependent on Chinese-made polysilicon, wafers, and cells, U.S. trade authorities determined the route was substantially circumventing China-specific duties and imposed steep new tariffs in 2024-2025, illustrating how quickly a single trade-enforcement action can reroute a multi-billion-dollar equipment supply chain.
historical_precedents: On August 23, 2023, the U.S. Department of Commerce made a final affirmative determination that crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells completed in Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, or Vietnam using Chinese-made parts and components were circumventing existing antidumping and countervailing duty orders on China, per the Federal Register.

On April 21, 2025, Commerce announced final antidumping and countervailing duty rates on solar cells and modules from the four countries, ranging up to 3,521% for Cambodia, 972% for Thailand, 814% for Vietnam, and 250% for Malaysia; following the U.S. International Trade Commission's June 9, 2025 affirmative injury determination, U.S. Customs and Border Protection began collecting the duties on June 16, 2025.

paths.name: China's Dominance in EV Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing
origin_regions: China (battery-cell manufacturing clusters in Fujian, Jiangsu, Guangdong, and other provinces)
chokepoints: Single-country concentration of battery cell manufacturing capacity in China (roughly 80-85% of global output/capacity)
Concentration of cathode active material (~85%) and anode active material (>90%) production in China
Technology-licensing dependency on Chinese cell chemistries (e.g., LFP) even for gigafactories built outside China
destination_regions: global EV and grid-storage battery-pack assembly (Europe, North America, Japan, South Korea)
paths.why_it_matters: China accounted for roughly 80% of global lithium-ion battery cell production in 2024 and supplies the large majority of the cathode and anode active materials that go into those cells, giving it outsized influence over EV and grid-storage battery costs worldwide. Two Chinese firms, CATL and BYD, alone held a combined majority of the global EV battery market in 2024, and the concentration runs deep enough that even automakers building battery plants in the United States and Europe, such as Ford's Michigan LFP plant, have relied on licensed Chinese cell technology rather than fully independent designs.
historical_precedents: In February 2023, Ford announced a $3.5 billion wholly owned lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery plant in Marshall, Michigan, built using battery technology licensed from China's CATL, illustrating how even U.S.-based, U.S.-owned battery manufacturing has depended on Chinese cell chemistry and process know-how.

Effective December 1, 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce required export permits for high-purity synthetic and spherical natural graphite products used in battery anodes, tightening a chokepoint the IEA says supplies over 90% of global anode active material processing.

paths.name: Global Wind Turbine Manufacturing Supply Concentration
chokepoints: Rapid buildout of Chinese domestic wind turbine manufacturing capacity, now roughly 60% of global manufacturing capacity
China's near-total (99.96%) domestic-market self-supply, limiting the pool of turbines independently price-tested outside China
EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation scrutiny of Chinese turbine suppliers bidding into European wind-farm tenders
paths.why_it_matters: Chinese wind turbine manufacturers have risen from about 30% of the global market in 2017 to supplying the five largest annual turbine installers worldwide for the first time in 2025, while the IEA separately estimates China holds roughly 60% of global wind-system manufacturing capacity. Because Chinese OEMs still install over 90% of their own output domestically, most of that capacity has not yet been fully tested in open international competition, and European regulators have opened a formal subsidy investigation into Chinese suppliers winning tenders in EU member states, adding a distinct regulatory chokepoint alongside the underlying manufacturing concentration.

On April 9, 2024, the European Commission announced the first ex-officio investigation under its Foreign Subsidies Regulation, targeting Chinese wind turbine suppliers bidding into wind-farm tenders in Spain, Greece, France, Romania, and Bulgaria; the Commission escalated to a formal in-depth second-stage investigation into Goldwind's EU activities in February 2026.

paths.name: China's Gallium and Germanium Export Controls on Semiconductor Materials
origin_regions: China (primary low-purity gallium production and refined germanium metal)
chokepoints: China's near-total dominance of primary low-purity gallium production, about 99% of world output
China's leading position in refined germanium metal production and export, with few alternative sources
Chinese Ministry of Commerce export-licensing requirements on gallium- and germanium-related items, in effect since August 2023
December 2024 Chinese ban on gallium and germanium exports specifically to the United States
destination_regions: United States, Japan, South Korea, and Europe (semiconductor, defense-electronics, fiber-optic, and solar-cell manufacturing)
paths.why_it_matters: Gallium and germanium are produced in small volumes worldwide but are essential inputs for compound semiconductors (gallium arsenide and gallium nitride) used in mobile-phone chips, radar and defense electronics, LEDs, and solar cells, as well as for germanium-based fiber optics and infrared optics. China dominates both the mining and refining of gallium and is the leading global producer of germanium, giving it outsized influence over the front end of semiconductor and optoelectronics supply chains at a time when both materials are also central to U.S.-China technology-trade tensions.
historical_precedents: In July 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs announced export-licensing controls on gallium- and germanium-related items, effective August 1, 2023, citing national security; China's monthly gallium and germanium export volumes fell sharply as licenses were slow to be granted, with China's germanium exports for the year through August 2024 down 55% year-on-year.

In December 2024, China's Commerce Ministry banned outright the export to the United States of gallium, germanium, antimony, and other materials with potential military applications, responding to expanded U.S. export controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment; the U.S. Geological Survey estimated a full ban could raise gallium prices by as much as 150% and germanium prices by about 26%, with billions of dollars in downstream economic effects.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for an estimated 99% of world primary low-purity gallium production in 2024 (about 750,000 of a 760,000-kilogram world total) and was the world's leading producer and exporter of germanium metal, per the U.S. Geological Survey; the United States was 100% import-reliant for gallium and more than 50% import-reliant for germanium in 2024, with China supplying 51% of U.S. germanium metal imports and 19% of U.S. gallium metal imports in 2020-2023.

paths.name: China's Antimony Export Controls and Global Price Shock
origin_regions: Russia, Tajikistan, Burma (Myanmar), and Bolivia (secondary mine production)
chokepoints: China's dominance of both antimony mine production and downstream oxide and metal processing
Chinese Ministry of Commerce export-licensing requirements on antimony ore, metals, oxides, and related items, effective September 15, 2024
December 2024 outright Chinese ban on antimony exports to the United States
destination_regions: global lead-acid battery, flame-retardant, ammunition, and optics/semiconductor manufacturing, concentrated in the United States, Europe, and East Asia
paths.why_it_matters: Antimony is a small-volume but strategically important metal used in flame retardants, lead-acid battery alloys, and more than 200 types of military munitions, as well as in some semiconductor and solar applications. China mines roughly three-fifths of the world's antimony and processes most of the rest into oxide and metal, so a single government's licensing decisions can rapidly tighten global supply. The 2024 export-control episode produced one of the sharpest price spikes of any critical mineral in recent years and prompted U.S. Department of Defense funding for a domestic antimony project.
historical_precedents: On August 15, 2024, China's Ministry of Commerce announced that exporters of antimony ore, metals, oxides, and related items would need export licenses and to declare end use, effective September 15, 2024; antimony metal prices roughly doubled within weeks, from about $8.91 per pound in July to $17.50 per pound in November 2024, according to Argus Media Group data cited by USGS.

In December 2024, China banned outright the export of antimony, along with gallium and germanium, to the United States; the metal's price, which had traded around $1,400 per metric ton in mid-2024, reached roughly $39,500-$40,000 per metric ton by the end of December 2024, an annual increase of about 250%.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for an estimated 34% of world antimony mine production in 2024 (40,000 of 119,000 metric tons, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026's finalized figures, which revised an initial 2025 estimate of 60,000/100,000/60%), but continues to hold the large majority of world antimony oxide and metal processing capacity -- the downstream stage where its export-licensing controls actually bite; the United States' net import reliance for antimony rose to 91% in 2025, with the average U.S. antimony price more than doubling to about $25 per pound (from $10.24 in 2024), per the U.S. Geological Survey.

paths.name: China's Dominance of Natural Graphite and Battery Anode Materials
commodities: natural graphite (flake and spherical, battery-anode grade)
origin_regions: Mozambique, Madagascar, Brazil, and Tanzania (mining, smaller volumes)
chokepoints: China's dominance of natural graphite mining, about 78% of world output
China's even greater dominance of downstream spherical, battery-anode-grade graphite processing
Chinese Ministry of Commerce export-licensing requirements on high-purity synthetic graphite and natural flake graphite, effective December 1, 2023
destination_regions: global lithium-ion battery and electric-vehicle manufacturing, concentrated in South Korea, Japan, Europe, and the United States
paths.why_it_matters: Graphite is the largest component by weight in the lithium-ion battery anodes used in EVs and grid storage, and it also underpins steelmaking, brake linings, and refractory applications. China not only mines the large majority of the world's natural graphite but also dominates the specialized processing that turns flake graphite into spherical, battery-grade material, making it one of the most concentrated links in the EV battery supply chain even though the raw ore itself is geographically widespread.
historical_precedents: On October 20, 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce announced export-permit requirements for high-purity, high-hardness, high-intensity synthetic graphite and for natural flake graphite and its products, effective December 1, 2023, citing national security; Chinese exports of flake and spherical graphite fell sharply in early 2024 as export licenses were slow to be issued, with spherical graphite exports down 65% year-on-year in the first two months of 2024.

In May 2024, the U.S. Department of the Treasury temporarily extended, through 2027, an exemption allowing Chinese-origin graphite in EV batteries to remain eligible for U.S. clean-vehicle tax credits, and the U.S. announced a tariff increase on Chinese natural graphite from 0% to 25% beginning in 2026, reflecting policymakers' concern about the concentration of anode-material supply in China.

Following a December 2024 petition, the U.S. Department of Commerce set preliminary antidumping duties of 93.50% and countervailing duties ranging from 11.58% to 721.03% on Chinese graphite anode active material in 2025, after the U.S. International Trade Commission made a less-than-fair-value determination -- a substantial U.S.-side import restriction that mirrors, from the demand side, the export-control chokepoint China itself imposed in 2023.
paths.estimated_global_share: China produced an estimated 82% of world natural graphite mine output in 2024 (1.27 million of 1.55 million metric tons, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026's finalized figures, up from an initial 78% estimate) and refines the large majority of the spherical, battery-grade graphite used in lithium-ion anodes, per the U.S. Geological Survey; the United States was 100% import-reliant for natural graphite, with about 43% of 2020-2023 imports sourced from China.

paths.name: South African Platinum Group Metals to Global Catalytic Converter Manufacturing
commodities: platinum-group metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium, and related elements)
chokepoints: South Africa's dominance of global platinum mine production and PGM reserves, concentrated almost entirely in the Bushveld Complex
Deep-level, labor-intensive mining methods vulnerable to strikes and to electricity-supply disruptions
Russia's dominance of mined palladium, concentrating both principal catalytic-converter metals in two countries
destination_regions: global automotive manufacturing in China, Europe, Japan, and the United States (catalytic converters); electronics, glass, and chemical-catalyst manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Platinum and palladium are the primary active materials in catalytic converters that reduce vehicle exhaust emissions, and platinum-group metals are also used in chemical catalysis, electronics, dental and medical devices, and jewelry. South Africa's Bushveld Complex holds the large majority of the world's known PGM resources and is mined mostly through deep, labor-intensive shafts, making global supply sensitive to South African labor disputes and to the reliability of South Africa's electricity grid, while palladium supply is separately concentrated in Russia.
historical_precedents: From January 23 to June 24, 2014, roughly 70,000 platinum-mine workers in South Africa's Rustenburg area, represented by the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union, staged a five-month wage strike against the country's three largest platinum producers, the longest and most costly strike in South African history; the stoppage cut South African platinum output by an estimated 40% (roughly 440,000 ounces), reduced the industry's revenue by an estimated R24.1 billion, and lowered national GDP growth by an estimated 1.3 percentage points in the first quarter of 2014.

In 2023 and 2024, recurring nationwide electricity load-shedding by South Africa's state utility repeatedly curtailed output at deep-level PGM mines, which require continuous power for ventilation and hoisting; South African PGM production fell 15.2% in 2022 as mining operations ran an estimated 20-30% under capacity because of power curtailments, and the U.S. Geological Survey cited load-shedding, alongside declining prices and higher deep-mining costs, among the factors behind further falls in South African PGM production in 2023 and 2024.
paths.estimated_global_share: South Africa held an estimated 78% of world platinum-group-metal reserves (63 million of more than 81 million kilograms) and accounted for about 71% of world platinum mine production in 2024 (120,000 of 170,000 kilograms), per the U.S. Geological Survey; South Africa supplied an estimated 45% of U.S. platinum imports and 32% of U.S. palladium imports in 2020-2023.

paths.name: Jordan Phosphate Export Corridor (Aqaba)
origin_regions: Eshidiya, Wadi Al Abiad, Al Hassa, and Al Ruseifa phosphate mines, Jordan
chokepoints: Jordan Phosphate Mines Company (JPMC) industrial complex and export terminal, Aqaba, Jordan (Red Sea coast)
Red Sea and Bab-el-Mandeb shipping lanes toward South and Southeast Asia
paths.why_it_matters: Jordan is the world's fifth-largest phosphate rock producer, but because its own agricultural sector is small, most of its output is exported, and state-owned Jordan Phosphate Mines Company (JPMC) describes itself as the world's second-largest phosphate exporter. Output from JPMC's four mines is consolidated at a single industrial complex and dedicated export terminal on the Red Sea south of Aqaba, so any disruption to that one site, or to Red Sea shipping past the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, affects a large share of the phosphate rock and DAP fertilizer reaching South and Southeast Asian farmers. India alone has historically taken more than 60% of JPMC's shipments, making Jordan a concentrated, single-country-dependent link in the phosphorus supply chain for the region.
historical_precedents: 2020-2021: JPMC's phosphate rock output rose from 8.9 million tons in 2020 to a record 10.0 million tons in 2021, and the value of Jordan's phosphate exports increased 55% to $532 million in 2021 from $343 million in 2020; India remained the leading destination for Jordanian phosphate rock exports in both years, followed by Indonesia, Brazil, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and Saudi Arabia (USGS, Minerals Yearbook: Jordan 2020-2021).

2018: India's IFFCO and Indian Potash Limited acquired a 37% equity stake in JPMC from the Brunei Investment Agency for $130 million, formalizing a long-term supply relationship under which about 60% of JPMC's production was already being exported to India at the time of the purchase (Jordan Phosphate Mines Company).
paths.estimated_global_share: Jordan produced an estimated 12.0 million of the world's 250 million metric tons of phosphate rock in 2024/2025 (about 5%) and holds roughly 820 million metric tons of phosphate rock reserves, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, which revised Jordan's reserve estimate down from the roughly 1.0 billion metric tons reported a year earlier.

paths.name: Global Sulfur and Sulfuric Acid Trade (Phosphate Fertilizer Feedstock)
origin_regions: Persian Gulf oil and gas refining centers (Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Iran)
Western Canada oil sands and natural-gas-processing region (Alberta)
chokepoints: Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf shipping lanes
Rail and port export network from Alberta to Vancouver and U.S. Gulf Coast terminals
Black Sea and Caspian shipping routes for Kazakh and Russian sulfur
paths.why_it_matters: Sulfur itself is not a plant nutrient, but sulfuric acid made from it is the essential reagent used to dissolve phosphate rock into phosphoric acid, the intermediate feedstock for DAP and MAP fertilizers; an estimated 90% of sulfur consumed worldwide is used in the form of sulfuric acid. Because sulfur is overwhelmingly recovered as a byproduct of oil and gas refining rather than mined directly, its supply is concentrated in fossil-fuel-processing regions -- the Persian Gulf states, Western Canada, Kazakhstan, and Russia -- that do not always coincide with where phosphate fertilizer is manufactured. Morocco and Saudi Arabia, both major phosphate fertilizer exporters, have limited domestic sulfur production and rely on imported sulfur to run their phosphoric acid plants, so disruption to Gulf refining output or Hormuz shipping constrains phosphate fertilizer output nearly as directly as a phosphate rock shortage would.
historical_precedents: 2024: Contract sulfur prices at Tampa, Florida rose from $69 per long ton at the start of the year to $116 per long ton by the fourth quarter, reflecting sharp swings in demand tied to phosphate fertilizer expansion and new battery-metals processing capacity (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2025 onward: USGS projected that sulfur production from the Middle East would increase starting in 2025 because of refinery upgrades and new projects, with new sulfur demand from phosphate fertilizer expansion concentrated in Africa and west Asia -- regions where Morocco's and Saudi Arabia's phosphoric acid capacity has been expanding (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: World sulfur production (all forms) was a finalized 83.9 million metric tons in 2024 (revised down from an initial 85.0 million ton estimate; 2025 was estimated at 84.0 million tons); Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, and Iran together accounted for roughly 19.8 million tons (about 24%), and Canada and Kazakhstan together accounted for roughly 9.8 million tons (about 12%), per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026. The International Fertilizer Association's IFASTAT platform separately estimates that the Strait of Hormuz corridor alone carries about 49% of global sulfur trade.

paths.name: China Fertilizer Export Restrictions (Urea and Phosphate/DAP)
origin_regions: Nitrogen and phosphate fertilizer manufacturing centers in China (Yunnan, Guizhou, Hubei, Sichuan, and other provinces)
chokepoints: China's customs inspection and quota (CIQ) export-licensing regime for fertilizers
Chinese seaports handling bulk fertilizer exports
paths.why_it_matters: China is the world's largest producer of phosphate rock and one of the largest producers of urea and phosphate fertilizers, but Chinese authorities periodically tighten or halt fertilizer exports, through customs inspections, quotas, or informal guidance, to keep domestic fertilizer prices low for the country's own farmers and protect food security. Because China supplies a large share of world urea and DAP trade in years when restrictions are relaxed, these policy shifts function as a chokepoint distinct from any physical bottleneck: when Chinese volumes are withdrawn from world markets, importing countries such as India, Brazil, and several African and Southeast Asian nations that had come to depend on relatively low-cost Chinese fertilizer must compete for supply from Middle Eastern, Russian, and North American producers, which measurably raises global prices.
historical_precedents: 2021-2024: Under an administrative export-control and inspection regime in place since late 2021, China's urea exports collapsed from about 5-6 million tons in 2021 to just 0.26 million tons in 2024, and DAP exports fell from a pre-restriction baseline of about 6.2 million tons per year to 4.6 million tons in 2024 (IFPRI, 'How Fertilizer Policies Could Exacerbate Hormuz Price Shocks').

2024-2025: China's nitrogen fertilizer exports fell more than 90% year-on-year in 2024 as authorities prioritized domestic price stability and supply security, while phosphate exports were further constrained by intensified customs inspections; restrictions persisted through the first half of 2025 before urea shipments partially resumed later in the year (World Bank, 'Fertilizer Markets Soften But Remain Constrained by Trade Policies,' December 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for an estimated 105 million of the world's 239 million metric tons of phosphate rock production in 2024 (about 44%), the largest of any country, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (which finalized the 2024 figures down from an initial 110M/240M/46% estimate published a year earlier). In years without export restrictions, China has supplied on the order of 5-6 million tons of urea and about 6.2 million tons of DAP annually to world export markets, per IFPRI analysis of trade data.

paths.name: Saudi Arabia (Ma'aden) Phosphate Fertilizer Export Corridor
origin_regions: Al Jalamid and Al Khabra phosphate mines, Northern Border Region, Saudi Arabia
Wa'ad Al Shamal mining and processing complex, Saudi Arabia
chokepoints: Rail corridor from Al Jalamid/Wa'ad Al Shamal mines in Saudi Arabia's Northern Border Region to Ras Al Khair Industrial City on the Gulf coast
Ras Al Khair phosphate and fertilizer processing and export complex, Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia
Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf shipping lanes
paths.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia has rapidly built a fully integrated phosphate fertilizer industry under state-controlled Ma'aden, mining phosphate rock deep inland in the Northern Border Region and moving it by dedicated rail across the country to the Ras Al Khair processing and export complex on the Gulf coast, from which finished DAP and MAP are shipped out through the Strait of Hormuz. This single rail-and-port corridor now carries one of the fastest-growing phosphate fertilizer supply chains in the world, and Saudi Arabia's ongoing capacity expansions are expected to make it the world's third-largest producer of phosphate fertilizers after China and Morocco. Because the entire mine-to-port chain funnels through Ras Al Khair and then through Hormuz, disruption at either point would affect fertilizer supply to South Asian and other import-dependent markets that increasingly rely on Saudi DAP and MAP.
historical_precedents: 2020-2022: Saudi Arabia was the world's fourth-ranked producer of diammonium phosphate (DAP), accounting for an estimated 9.4% of world output in 2022, while combined DAP/MAP production capacity at Ma'aden Phosphate Co. and Ma'aden Wa'ad Al Shamal Phosphate Co. exceeded 6.2 million tons per year from 2020 onward (USGS, Minerals Yearbook: Saudi Arabia 2022 [Advance Release]).

2022-2025: Ma'aden continued construction of a third expansion phase at Wa'ad Al Shamal intended to add 3 million tons per year of DAP capacity, raising the company's total phosphate fertilizer production capacity to about 9 million tons per year on a completion date expected in 2025; the expansion was projected to make Saudi Arabia the world's third-ranked phosphate fertilizer producer, after China and Morocco (USGS, Minerals Yearbook: Saudi Arabia 2022 [Advance Release]).
paths.estimated_global_share: Saudi Arabia produced an estimated 10.0 million of the world's 250 million metric tons of phosphate rock in 2024/2025 (about 4%) and holds roughly 1.0 billion metric tons of phosphate rock reserves, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (which revised the 2024 production figure up from an initial 9.5 million ton estimate); in 2023 it remained the world's fourth-ranked DAP producer, at about 9.4% of world output, per USGS Minerals Yearbook: Saudi Arabia 2023 [Advance Release].

paths.name: Netherlands' ASML Semiconductor Lithography Equipment Route
origin_regions: Veldhoven, Netherlands (ASML headquarters and primary assembly)
chokepoints: ASML's effective global monopoly on EUV lithography systems (100% of world supply)
Dutch government export-licensing controls on advanced lithography equipment (expanded September 2024)
Single-company concentration of the ultra-precision optics, mechatronics, and light-source subsystems required to produce leading-edge chips
destination_regions: global advanced-logic and memory chip fabs
paths.why_it_matters: Every leading-edge logic and memory chip in the world, regardless of which country fabricates it, is patterned using lithography machines built by a single Dutch company, ASML, which is the sole global producer of EUV systems and a dominant producer of high-end DUV systems. This is a distinct chokepoint from the chip-fabrication routes themselves (Taiwan, South Korea): it sits one layer upstream, at the capital-equipment stage, so a disruption to ASML's production or to its ability to ship equipment affects the buildout of new fab capacity everywhere, not just output from existing fabs. Because EUV technology took ASML roughly three decades and billions of dollars of R&D to perfect, and involves components sourced from a small number of specialized suppliers (such as Zeiss optics from Germany), no rival has matched it, making Dutch export policy toward China a direct lever on the pace of Chinese advanced-chip development.
historical_precedents: Effective September 7, 2024, the Dutch government expanded its national export-control measure to require case-by-case authorization for exporting additional categories of advanced DUV immersion lithography equipment (including older TWINSCAN NXT:1970i/1980i models), building on restrictions first introduced in September 2023, citing security risks from equipment potentially enabling military-relevant chip production.

ASML has never shipped a single EUV system to China, having been effectively barred from doing so since 2018-2019; even so, China accounted for 41% of ASML's system sales in 2024 (almost entirely DUV tools) before falling to 23% in 2025 and roughly a fifth of expected 2026 revenue, as tightening Dutch and U.S. export licensing requirements took fuller effect.
paths.estimated_global_share: ASML is the world's sole producer of EUV lithography systems (effectively 100% global share) and one of only three global suppliers of lithography tools overall, alongside Nikon and Canon of Japan, per CSIS analysis; China's leading domestic lithography maker, Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment (SMEE), holds only about 4% of the global market and remains confined to legacy i-line/DUV tools.

paths.name: China, South Korea, and Japan Global Shipbuilding Concentration
origin_regions: China (Jiangsu, Liaoning, and Shanghai shipyard clusters)
South Korea (Ulsan and Geoje shipyard clusters)
chokepoints: Three-country concentration of over 95% of global merchant shipbuilding output
China's majority share of global newbuild capacity and contracting
U.S. Section 301 port fees and proposed tariffs on China-linked or China-built vessels (phased in from late 2025)
destination_regions: global merchant shipping lines and vessel-owning fleets worldwide
paths.why_it_matters: Nearly the entire world's supply of new merchant ships, the vessels that physically carry over 80% of global trade by volume, is built in just three countries. This is a distinct chokepoint from the canal and strait routes those ships sail through: it concerns the ability to build and replace the global fleet itself. Because switching shipyards involves years of lead time and limited spare capacity elsewhere, trade-policy actions or shipyard disruptions affecting any of the three countries, especially China given its outsized share, can raise newbuild prices, delay fleet renewal and decarbonization timelines, and reshape which yards shipowners are willing to contract with.
historical_precedents: On April 17, 2025, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative announced Section 301 port fees on vessels owned, operated, or built by China-linked entities (phasing in from October 2025), alongside proposed tariffs of up to 100% on China-built ship-to-shore cranes and China-origin shipping containers and chassis, following a year-long investigation into China's targeting of the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors for dominance.

China's share of global newbuild ship contracting fell from about 72% in the second half of 2024 to about 52% in the first half of 2025, a drop that shipping association BIMCO attributed in part to shipowner concern over the incoming USTR port fees, even as analysts noted limited shipbuilding capacity exists outside China to absorb the shift.

paths.name: Mexico-U.S. USMCA Nearshoring Manufacturing Corridor
origin_regions: Northern Mexico industrial corridor (Nuevo Leon, Chihuahua, Baja California, Coahuila, Tamaulipas)
Bajio region, Mexico (Guanajuato, Queretaro, San Luis Potosi)

USMCA rules-of-origin certification and compliance requirements

paths.why_it_matters: Mexico has become the anchor of a North American nearshoring corridor built around tight, truck-based cross-border manufacturing rather than long ocean voyages, making it structurally different from the Asia-origin routes covered elsewhere in this dataset. Mexico was the United States' top trading partner for a second consecutive year in 2024, and the corridor has become increasingly formalized: as new U.S. tariffs on non-USMCA-qualifying goods took effect in 2025, manufacturers rapidly restructured supply chains and paperwork to meet regional-content rules, causing the share of Mexican exports receiving USMCA preferential treatment to nearly double within a year. Because so much just-in-time automotive, electronics, and machinery production now depends on same-day or next-day truck crossings, disruptions at the border crossings themselves, or shifts in USMCA rules-of-origin policy, can quickly affect assembly lines on both sides of the border.
historical_precedents: Full-year 2024 U.S. Census Bureau trade data show Mexico as the top single-country U.S. trading partner for the second consecutive year, with $839.9 billion in total trade (15.8% of all U.S. trade) - the highest annual bilateral trade total the U.S. has recorded with any country.

Following new U.S. tariffs on goods not qualifying for USMCA preferential treatment, the share of Mexican exports receiving USMCA preference rose from 44.8% in January 2025 to 88.7% by November 2025, per U.S. Department of Commerce data, as exporters restructured sourcing to meet regional-content requirements.

A Federal Reserve Board analysis of USMCA automotive trade found that rules-of-origin compliance costs (documentation and sourcing adjustments) added an estimated 1.4 to 2.5 percentage points in ad valorem-equivalent cost to qualifying imports, illustrating that nearshoring under USMCA carries real compliance overhead even when it avoids tariffs.

paths.name: Global Power Transformer Manufacturing Shortage and Grid-Equipment Bottleneck
chokepoints: Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) meeting current U.S. Department of Energy transformer-core specifications can only be produced in three countries worldwide: Japan, South Korea, and Germany

The United States imported 82% of the large power transformers it consumed in 2019, and its sole remaining domestic GOES producer, Cleveland-Cliffs, has been unable to match imported material on quality or price

Average lead times for large power transformers have roughly doubled since 2021 and now extend up to four years, driven by surging demand from grid modernization, renewable interconnection, and data-center buildout
destination_regions: global electricity grid operators interconnecting new wind and solar capacity
paths.why_it_matters: Power transformers are the unglamorous chokepoint underlying the entire renewable-energy buildout: every wind or solar farm needs step-up transformers to connect to the grid, and every substation expansion needed to absorb new clean-energy capacity needs large power transformers, yet global manufacturing of both the finished units and their core material, grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES), is concentrated in a handful of countries. The U.S. Department of Energy found imports supplied 82% of large power transformers consumed in the United States in 2019, while GOES capable of meeting DOE efficiency specifications is produced only in Japan, South Korea, and Germany. The IEA's 2025 assessment found lead times for large power transformers have nearly doubled since 2021 to as long as four years, and Wood Mackenzie projects a 30% supply deficit for power transformers in 2025 alone, a bottleneck now cited by developers and utilities as a binding constraint on how fast new renewable capacity can actually be connected to the grid.
historical_precedents: In February 2022, the U.S. Department of Energy published its Electric Grid Supply Chain Review of Large Power Transformers and High Voltage Direct Current Systems (mandated by Executive Order 14017), finding that imports accounted for 82% of large power transformers consumed in the United States in 2019, that the six U.S. manufacturers were operating at only about 40% capacity utilization, and that only Japan, South Korea, and Germany could produce GOES meeting DOE specifications.

In February 2025, the IEA's Building the Future Transmission Grid report found that average lead times for large power transformers and high-voltage cables had almost doubled since 2021, with the largest power transformers taking up to four years to procure and prices up substantially since 2019.
paths.estimated_global_share: The United States imported 82% of the large power transformers it consumed in 2019, per the U.S. Department of Energy's 2022 supply chain assessment; Wood Mackenzie estimated in August 2025 that the U.S. market would face a 30% supply deficit for power transformers and a 10% deficit for distribution transformers in 2025, with average lead times of 128 weeks for power transformers and 144 weeks for generator step-up transformers as of its second-quarter 2025 survey.

chokepoints: China's share of global electrolyzer manufacturing capacity rose from about 5% in 2019 to nearly 60% by 2025, per the IEA
China controls an estimated 85% of global alkaline water electrolyzer (AWE) manufacturing capacity, the dominant technology in large-scale green hydrogen projects
China's annual electrolyzer manufacturing capacity of roughly 20 GW is far above global demand of about 2 GW a year, creating overcapacity that undercuts non-Chinese manufacturers on price

paths.why_it_matters: China's electrolyzer manufacturers have gone from a marginal presence to supplying the majority of the equipment underpinning the global green hydrogen buildout in under a decade: the IEA found China's share of global electrolyzer manufacturing capacity rose from about 5% in 2019 to nearly 60% in 2025, and six of the world's top ten electrolyzer manufacturers by capacity are now Chinese-headquartered. Because Chinese manufacturing capacity of roughly 20 GW a year already far exceeds current global demand of about 2 GW, Chinese suppliers can set a price floor that makes it difficult for European, Japanese, and North American manufacturers to compete on cost, even as some Chinese-made equipment has shown real-world performance shortfalls: Sinopec's 260-megawatt Kuqa green hydrogen facility in Xinjiang, one of the world's largest, has run at under a third of its rated capacity in part because its electrolyzers struggle to handle the variable power output of an attached solar array.

paths.name: China's Dominance in Grid-Scale Battery Storage (BESS) Manufacturing

battery energy storage system (BESS) containers and integrated systems
origin_regions: China (CATL, BYD, Hithium, EVE Energy, Sungrow, CALB, REPT BATTERO)
chokepoints: All ten of the world's largest BESS cell suppliers by 2025 shipment volume were headquartered in China, together accounting for more than 90% of global cell shipments
China supplied close to 60% of new grid-scale battery storage capacity installed worldwide in 2025

US Section 301 tariff on lithium-ion batteries other than for electric passenger vehicles, the HTS line covering grid-storage cells, rising to 25% effective January 1, 2026, stacking on top of existing reciprocal tariffs
paths.why_it_matters: Grid-scale battery storage has become the fastest-growing piece of the energy transition's equipment stack, needed to firm intermittent wind and solar output and increasingly to back up data-center power demand, and China's grip on that supply chain is now even tighter than in EV batteries: all ten of the world's largest BESS cell suppliers by 2025 shipment volume, led by CATL, Hithium, and EVE Energy, were headquartered in China, together shipping more than 90% of the cells installed worldwide, while South Korean cell makers LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI, which remain competitive in EV batteries, fell entirely out of the top ten. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry, where China holds the deepest cost and manufacturing advantage, made up about 90% of 2025 BESS deployments. The United States has responded with a trade-policy track distinct from EV batteries: a Section 301 tariff specifically on non-EV lithium-ion batteries is set to reach 25% on January 1, 2026, and in December 2024 U.S. producers filed the first antidumping and countervailing duty petition targeting battery materials embedded within finished battery products, alleging Chinese anode-material dumping margins as high as 921%.

On September 18, 2024, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative published a Federal Register notice finalizing Section 301 tariff increases that raised duties on lithium-ion electric-vehicle batteries to 25% effective 2024 and set duties on lithium-ion batteries other than for electric vehicles, the category covering grid-storage cells, to rise to 25% effective January 1, 2026.

On December 18, 2024, the American Active Anode Material Producers filed antidumping and countervailing duty petitions alleging Chinese battery anode material was being dumped into the U.S. market at margins of up to 921%; the U.S. Department of Commerce initiated the investigation on January 15, 2025.

paths.name: U.S. Coal Exports from Appalachia and the Powder River Basin
origin_regions: United States (Central and Northern Appalachia: West Virginia, Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Virginia; Powder River Basin: Wyoming, Montana)
chokepoints: East Coast export terminals at Norfolk, Virginia (including the Lambert's Point terminal) and Baltimore, Maryland, which together handle the majority of U.S. coal exports
Gulf Coast terminals at Mobile, Alabama and New Orleans, Louisiana

Absence of a large-capacity U.S. West Coast coal export terminal after a wave of Pacific Northwest terminal proposals was cancelled in the 2010s, leaving Powder River Basin coal bound for Asia dependent on Canadian terminals near Vancouver and Prince Rupert, British Columbia
Concentrated buyer exposure, in which a small number of destination countries account for a large share of exports, so a single country's tariff action can swing total export volumes
paths.why_it_matters: The United States is a mid-sized but strategically flexible coal exporter, shipping both thermal coal (mostly Powder River Basin subbituminous coal used for power generation) and metallurgical coal (mostly Appalachian coal used in steelmaking) to markets across Asia, Europe, Africa, and Latin America. Because the U.S. has no large operating coal export terminal on the Pacific coast, after a wave of proposed Pacific Northwest terminals was cancelled in the 2010s amid local opposition and weak economics, most Powder River Basin coal bound for Asia must travel via Canadian rail and port routes near Vancouver and Prince Rupert, British Columbia, rather than exporting directly from the U.S. West Coast; Appalachian coal instead moves mainly through Atlantic and Gulf Coast ports at Norfolk, Baltimore, Mobile, and New Orleans. That leaves U.S. coal exports acting as a swing supplier to global markets, filling gaps left by supply disruptions elsewhere, but also exposed to abrupt shifts in a small number of buyer countries' trade policy, as shown when new Chinese tariffs cut U.S. coal exports to China by 92% in 2025.
historical_precedents: U.S. coal exports rose for four consecutive years to a six-year high of 108 million short tons in 2024, before falling 16 million short tons to 93 million short tons in 2025 after China imposed a 15% additional tariff on U.S. goods in February 2025 and a 34% reciprocal tariff in April 2025; the tariffs cut U.S. coal exports to China by 92% year-over-year and contributed to an 18% drop in U.S. thermal coal exports and an 11% drop in metallurgical coal exports for the year, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In the 2010s, developers proposed several coal export terminals for the Pacific Northwest, including the Gateway Pacific Terminal and Millennium Bulk Terminals projects in Washington State, intended to ship Powder River Basin coal directly to Asia; all had been cancelled or denied permits by 2017 amid local and tribal opposition, permitting disputes, and weak coal-price economics, leaving Canadian terminals at Roberts Bank and Prince Rupert, British Columbia as the primary maritime gateway for Powder River Basin coal exports to Asia, per the Congressional Research Service's 'U.S. Coal Exports' report.
paths.estimated_global_share: The United States exported 108 million short tons of coal in 2024, of which steam (thermal) coal accounted for 48% (51.7 million short tons); exports fell to 93 million short tons in 2025 as Chinese tariffs curtailed purchases. In 2022, U.S. coal exports of about 85.9 million short tons equaled roughly 14% of domestic coal production and reached 71 countries, with India, the Netherlands, Japan, Brazil, and South Korea the leading destinations; over 2021-2025, East Coast ports handled 62% of U.S. coal exports, Gulf Coast ports 25%, and West Coast ports 8%, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: South Africa's Richards Bay Coal Corridor to Asia
chokepoints: Transnet Freight Rail's coal export line linking Mpumalanga mines to the coast, historically constrained by locomotive shortages
Richards Bay Coal Terminal (RBCT) in KwaZulu-Natal, the dedicated export facility with installed rail-receiving capacity of about 91 million tonnes a year
Copper-cable theft and vandalism along the rail corridor
paths.why_it_matters: South Africa's coal exports funnel almost entirely through a single rail corridor and terminal: Transnet Freight Rail's coal line from the Mpumalanga coalfields to the Richards Bay Coal Terminal (RBCT) on the KwaZulu-Natal coast. Because that link is a near-monopoly chokepoint, degradation of Transnet's freight-rail performance, from locomotive shortages to widespread copper-cable theft, cut RBCT's exports nearly in half even though the terminal's installed rail-receiving capacity of about 91 million tonnes a year was never the binding constraint; mine output and international demand were available, but the trains could not reliably reach the coast. The subsequent recovery, driven by new locomotives and anti-theft measures rather than new mines or new demand, illustrates how logistics infrastructure, more than resource endowment, has become the primary swing factor in South Africa's ability to serve Asian coal buyers, chiefly India, which now takes the large majority of its seaborne coal.
historical_precedents: Richards Bay Coal Terminal exports fell for six consecutive years from a record 76.47 million tonnes in 2017 to a 32-year low of 47.21 million tonnes in 2023, a decline driven by Transnet Freight Rail locomotive shortages, unplanned infrastructure failures, and copper-cable theft and vandalism along the coal line, per Mining Weekly and Richards Bay Coal Terminal.

Following a November 2023 cooperation agreement between RBCT and Transnet, the phased replacement of underperforming locomotives with French-built Alstom 23E units, and expanded drone, foot, and K9 anti-theft patrols that cut copper-cable theft along the line from about 180 km stolen in 2024 to 59 km in 2025, RBCT exports rose more than 10% in successive years, reaching 52.08 million tonnes in 2024 and 57.66 million tonnes in 2025, per Daily Maverick and Mining Weekly.
paths.estimated_global_share: South Africa exported about 70.92 million tonnes of coal of all types in 2024 and 71.86 million tonnes in 2025, of which the large majority moved through Richards Bay Coal Terminal (52.08 million tonnes in 2024; 57.66 million tonnes in 2025); by 2025 nearly 80% of RBCT's coal went to Asian buyers, with India taking the largest share, followed by Europe (about 7%) and North Africa, chiefly Morocco (about 7%), per Mysteel and Daily Maverick.

paths.name: Russia's Coal Export Reorientation to Asia
chokepoints: Eastbound rail capacity on the Trans-Siberian Railway and Baikal-Amur Mainline (BAM), which link Siberian coal basins to Pacific ports and are approaching their operating capacity limits
Pacific coast export terminals, chiefly Vostochny Port near Nakhodka, Russia's largest coal terminal
European Union and allied-government sanctions restricting Russian coal's traditional westbound markets
paths.why_it_matters: Russia was, until 2022, one of the world's largest coal exporters, shipping roughly even volumes to European and Asian buyers. A European Union sanctions package banning imports of Russian coal took full effect in August 2022, eliminating what had been a major export market within months; Europe's share of Russia's coal exports fell from 32% in 2020 to just 13% by 2024, with Turkey (outside the EU) becoming the largest remaining European buyer. Russian exporters redirected shipments toward China, India, and South Korea, but the shift depends on rail lines built for a much smaller eastbound trade: the Trans-Siberian Railway and Baikal-Amur Mainline, along with Pacific coast terminals such as Vostochny Port, are now close to their operating capacity, so eastbound growth slowed to roughly 6% a year in 2024-2025 even as rail freight tariffs on export routes rose sharply. The result is that total Russian coal export volumes have kept falling even as the Asian share of what remains keeps growing, illustrating how a market's transport geography, not just its total production, determines how quickly an exporter can absorb the loss of a major buyer region.
historical_precedents: The European Union's fifth sanctions package, adopted in April 2022, banned imports of Russian coal and other solid fossil fuels effective August 2022, a ban the European Commission estimated would affect about 4 billion euros a year in trade; Europe's share of Russia's coal exports subsequently fell from 32% in 2020 to 13% in 2024, per the European Council and the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Russia's total rail-borne coal exports fell from a peak of 224.5 million tonnes in 2021 to 190.7 million tonnes in 2025, even as eastbound shipments toward Asia grew to 118.4 million tonnes (62% of the total) in 2025 and overtook westbound volumes, because growth on the capacity-constrained Trans-Siberian Railway and Baikal-Amur Mainline slowed to about 6% a year in 2024-2025 and could not fully offset the loss of European buyers, per trade publication The Coal Hub.
paths.estimated_global_share: China received slightly more than half of Russia's total coal exports in 2024, while Indian purchases of Russian coal nearly tripled from about 9.1 million short tons in 2020 to about 24.8 million short tons in 2024, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: China's Concentration of Crude (Porcine) Heparin Raw Material Supply
origin_regions: China (hog-slaughter and heparin crude-extraction network tied to China's large-scale pig processing industry)
chokepoints: China supplies an estimated 80% of the world's crude heparin active ingredient, extracted as a byproduct of pig-intestine processing at Chinese slaughterhouses

A U.S. regulatory prohibition on bovine (cattle)-derived heparin, adopted roughly two decades ago over mad-cow-disease (BSE) concerns, eliminated the main alternative animal source and locked global supply into a single species and country
Fragmented, small-scale collection of raw intestinal mucosa across a large number of Chinese slaughterhouses and workshops, which complicates quality control and traceability of the crude material
No comparable domestic U.S. collection-and-processing infrastructure exists despite the United States being one of the world's largest pork producers
paths.why_it_matters: China supplies roughly 80% of the world's crude heparin and about 74% of the heparin used in the United States, according to a Council on Foreign Relations supply-chain analysis. Heparin is an unsynthesized biologic extract rather than a chemically manufactured API, so it cannot simply be produced at a new factory; it depends on the volume and consistency of a country's pig-slaughter industry, which is why it appears on the WHO, HHS, FDA, and U.S. Department of Defense critical/essential medicines lists and supports an estimated 265 million doses administered to more than 12 million hospitalized Americans each year. Because a 1990s-era U.S. ban on bovine-derived heparin removed the one alternative animal source, there is no readily available substitute species or country if Chinese supply is disrupted by animal disease, trade friction, or a slaughterhouse-industry shock.
historical_precedents: On 30 July 2019, bipartisan leaders of the U.S. House Energy and Commerce Committee sent a letter to the FDA requesting a briefing on the threat that African swine fever, which had by then killed a large share of China's pig population, posed to the U.S. heparin supply, citing an expert estimate that 'nearly 80 percent of the world's heparin ingredient supply is made in China' and noting that past animal-disease outbreaks suggested a six-to-nine-month lag before a shortage would reach the U.S. market.

On 7 October 2019, the FDA publicly confirmed it had contacted U.S. heparin manufacturers directly and that the majority reported no supply disruption from African swine fever at that time, while stating it would continue monitoring the situation closely - illustrating that the degree of single-country, single-species concentration was severe enough to prompt a formal U.S. government risk-monitoring response even before any actual shortage materialized.
paths.estimated_global_share: China supplies an estimated 80% of the world's crude heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient and about 74% of the finished heparin used in the United States, per a Council on Foreign Relations supply-chain analysis; the U.S. has no domestic bovine-heparin alternative following a decades-old FDA prohibition adopted over BSE (mad-cow-disease) concerns.

paths.name: Global Insulin Manufacturing Concentration Among Three Multinational Producers
chokepoints: Three multinational companies - Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly, and Sanofi - control more than 90% of the global insulin market by value, and hold more than 95% market share in a majority of the lower-income countries studied by the World Health Organization
High capital cost, regulatory complexity, and biologic-manufacturing expertise required to produce insulin at scale, which limits new entrants and generic or biosimilar competition

Corporate manufacturing-capacity allocation decisions, including shifting production lines toward higher-margin GLP-1 diabetes and obesity drugs, which can affect the continued availability of older insulin products
Inconsistent registration of WHO-listed essential insulins in many national drug-regulatory systems, leaving few alternative suppliers if one manufacturer discontinues or delays a product

paths.why_it_matters: Three companies - Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly, and Sanofi - control more than 90% of the global insulin market by value, and in 19 of 32 lower- and middle-income countries studied hold more than 95% market share, according to a November 2021 World Health Organization report marking the 100th anniversary of insulin's discovery. The same report found that one out of every two people who need insulin for type 2 diabetes does not receive it. Because insulin manufacturing is capital-intensive, tightly regulated, and geographically concentrated in a handful of production networks based mainly in Denmark, the United States, France, and Germany, a commercial decision by any one of the three dominant producers to discontinue a product line, reprioritize manufacturing capacity, or exit a national market can leave patients in that market with few or no alternative suppliers.
historical_precedents: As documented on the European Medicines Agency's shortages register (first published 31 October 2025), Novo Nordisk decided for commercial and manufacturing-capacity reasons to discontinue multiple human insulin presentations (including Actrapid, Insulatard, Mixtard, and Levemir) across all EU/EEA member states, with discontinuation to take effect before the end of 2026; the EMA stated the decision was 'not related to a quality defect or safety issue' and advised prescribers to transition patients to alternative insulins with close glucose monitoring.

As separately documented on the EMA's shortages register (first published 23 March 2026), Eli Lilly announced it would discontinue several human insulin, insulin lispro, and insulin glargine presentations - including Humalog Mix25 across all EU/EEA markets where it was sold - for commercial reasons, with discontinuations expected by the second quarter of 2027; the near-simultaneous commercial exits of two of the world's three dominant insulin producers from specific product lines within about a five-month span illustrate how thin the alternative-supplier base is once a manufacturer decides to withdraw a product.
paths.estimated_global_share: Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly, and Sanofi together control more than 90% of the global insulin market by value, and hold more than 95% market share in 19 of 32 lower- and middle-income countries studied, per a November 2021 World Health Organization report.

paths.name: United States Source Plasma Collection and Global Plasma-Derived Medicine Export Dominance
commodities: plasma-derived medicinal products (immunoglobulin, albumin, clotting factors)
chokepoints: The United States hosts the large majority of the world's plasma collection centers and is one of the few countries that permits large-scale compensated (paid) plasma donation, making it the source of an estimated 70% of the plasma used to manufacture plasma-derived medicines worldwide

Plasma-derived medicine manufacturing is a lengthy fractionation process that can take up to a year from donation to finished product, so a drop in donations does not surface as a finished-product shortage until many months later
Most other countries, including across the European Union, remain far from self-sufficient in plasma and depend on imported U.S. plasma or U.S.-derived finished products
A small number of large plasma-fractionation companies process the bulk of collected plasma into finished immunoglobulin, albumin, and clotting-factor products
destination_regions: global markets for immunoglobulin, albumin, and clotting-factor therapies
paths.why_it_matters: The United States supplies an estimated 70% of the plasma used worldwide to manufacture plasma-derived medicinal products such as immunoglobulin, albumin, and clotting factors, because it is one of the only countries that allows donors to be compensated for plasma at scale, according to a peer-reviewed review of global plasma supply sustainability. Because manufacturing these products from raw plasma into finished medicine can take up to a year, and because most other countries - the European Union's plasma self-sufficiency rate fell to roughly 15% in 2022 - depend on U.S.-collected plasma or imported plasma products, a sustained drop in American donation volumes does not show up as a global shortage until long after the underlying cause, making the supply chain difficult to correct quickly once disrupted.
historical_precedents: U.S. source-plasma collections fell from approximately 53.5 million donations in 2019 to approximately 43.8 million in 2021, a roughly 20% decline, as COVID-19 social-distancing measures and reduced foot traffic curtailed visits to donation centers; because plasma-derived medicine manufacturing lags collection by up to a year, the resulting tightness in immunoglobulin and other plasma-product supply persisted into the latter half of 2022, according to a peer-reviewed supply-sustainability review and a companion clinical report on the pandemic's effect on source-plasma donations.

A 2024 global survey of hospital immunoglobulin providers across the United States, Canada, Europe, Japan, and Australia, conducted by the BEST Collaborative and published in the journal Transfusion, found that more than 60% of responding hospitals reported immunoglobulin supply shortages and that most sites had not developed formal mitigation strategies, illustrating how concentrated dependence on U.S.-sourced plasma leaves many countries' hospital systems exposed simultaneously when American collection volumes fluctuate.

paths.name: China-Concentrated Iodinated Contrast Media (CT Imaging Dye) Manufacturing
commodities: radiology and CT imaging contrast dye
chokepoints: A single GE Healthcare facility in Shanghai produced roughly 80% of GE Healthcare's global iohexol and iodixanol contrast-media supply, and more than half of all iodinated contrast used in the United States, prior to 2022
Only one secondary GE Healthcare production site (Cork, Ireland) existed as backup capacity, and competing contrast-media manufacturers lacked spare capacity to quickly absorb a large supply gap
Hospitals' and radiology departments' historically thin, one-to-two-week inventory buffers for contrast media, maintained for cost reasons, left little cushion against a production interruption
Iodinated contrast has no simple substitute for many CT and interventional-radiology procedures, so imaging and diagnostic capacity itself becomes constrained when supply tightens
destination_regions: global hospital radiology and cardiology departments
paths.why_it_matters: Iodinated contrast media is used in tens of millions of CT scans and interventional radiology procedures worldwide each year, and before 2022 roughly 80% of GE Healthcare's global supply of it - and more than half of all iodinated contrast used in the United States - came from a single manufacturing facility in Shanghai, China, according to a March 2023 Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH) health technology review. Because hospitals typically hold only one to two weeks of contrast inventory and because no other manufacturer had spare capacity to absorb a large supply gap, a localized public-health measure on the other side of the world was able to force hospitals across North America and Europe to ration or postpone imaging-dependent diagnosis and treatment within weeks.
historical_precedents: On 31 March 2022, a city-wide COVID-19 lockdown in Shanghai forced GE Healthcare to close its iodinated-contrast manufacturing facility there for several weeks; in an April 19, 2022 letter to customers, GE Healthcare said it was rationing orders and expected roughly an 80% cut in fulfillment through the end of June, prompting the FDA to list iohexol and iodixanol contrast products as in shortage in May 2022 and Health Canada to add them to its Tier 3 (greatest potential impact) shortage list in June 2022; U.S. hospitals postponed non-urgent CT scans, including cancer treatment-monitoring imaging, and adopted contrast-conservation protocols during the shortage, according to the Radiological Society of North America.

GE Healthcare restored its Shanghai facility to full production on 8 June 2022 after expanding output at its Cork, Ireland plant and accelerating air shipments to the United States, but global supply did not fully restabilize for several more weeks, illustrating how quickly a single-site disruption of this scale can outpace the contrast-media industry's ability to reroute production.
paths.estimated_global_share: A single GE Healthcare facility in Shanghai supplied roughly 80% of GE Healthcare's global iohexol/iodixanol contrast media output, and more than half of all iodinated contrast used in the United States, prior to the 2022 disruption, per a March 2023 Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH) health technology review.

paths.name: Turkish Straits (Bosphorus and Dardanelles) Oil Transit Corridor
chokepoints: Bosphorus Strait
Dardanelles Strait
paths.why_it_matters: The Bosphorus and Dardanelles together form the only sea link between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, giving Russian and Caspian Sea (Kazakh, Azerbaijani) oil exporters their most direct route to European and world markets. The waterways are less than half a nautical mile wide at their narrowest point and wind through the middle of Istanbul, a city of more than 15 million people, making them among the most difficult and heavily trafficked straits in the world to navigate; more than 45,000 vessels transited in 2024. Unlike most other major oil chokepoints, there is no pipeline bypass of comparable capacity, so congestion, weather, or a serious accident can back up tanker traffic for days.
historical_precedents: On 13 March 1994, the tanker Nassia collided with the cargo ship Shipbroker near the northern end of the Bosphorus; the resulting fire and explosions killed 24 crew and spilled an estimated 95,000 tonnes of crude oil, one of the worst accidents in the strait's history. The disaster led Turkish authorities to introduce a formal vessel traffic separation scheme for the strait.

EIA data show Kazakhstan and Russia jointly increased crude oil and condensate volumes sent through the Turkish Straits by about 400,000 barrels per day between 2022 and the first half of 2025, underscoring the corridor's growing role as Caspian and Russian output has risen.
paths.estimated_global_share: About 3.7 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum products transited the Turkish Straits in the first half of 2025 (roughly 5% of global maritime-traded oil), with crude oil and condensate making up about 60% of that volume; Kazakhstan is the largest single exporter through the straits, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
