paths.name: Norway North Sea Natural Gas Pipeline Network to Europe
origin_regions: Norway (North Sea, Norwegian Sea, and Barents Sea offshore fields)
chokepoints: Gassco-operated pipeline network (Europipe 1/2, Norpipe, Franpipe, Zeepipe, and related lines)
Kårstø gas processing hub
paths.why_it_matters: Norway became Europe's largest single supplier of natural gas after Russian pipeline deliveries to the continent collapsed following 2022, and it now delivers roughly 30% of Europe's gas imports through an 8,800-kilometer subsea pipeline network operated by the state-owned company Gassco. Because this network directly connects offshore fields to landing points in the UK, Germany, France, Belgium, and the Netherlands with no intervening strait or third-country transit, it carries a different risk profile than most chokepoint routes: its main vulnerabilities are field decline, planned/unplanned maintenance outages, and physical security of subsea infrastructure rather than shipping-lane disruption.
historical_precedents: In March 2022, amid a sharp reduction in Russian pipeline gas deliveries to Europe, the Norwegian government authorized an increase of about 50 billion cubic feet in natural gas production, primarily from the Oseberg and Heidrun fields, to help fill the resulting supply gap, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Norway's pipeline gas exports to Europe rose 7.8% in 2024 to a record 117.6 billion cubic meters, edging out the previous record of 117.4 billion cubic meters set in 2017, according to Gassco figures reported by Reuters.
paths.estimated_global_share: Norway supplied about 30% of Europe's natural gas imports in 2024 via pipeline, delivering a record 117.6 billion cubic meters (about 95% of its total gas exports) through its 8,800-km Gassco-operated pipeline network, per Reuters reporting on Gassco data and the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Norway Country Analysis Brief.

paths.name: Australia LNG Exports to Northeast Asia
chokepoints: Western Australia LNG processing hubs (Gorgon, Wheatstone, Ichthys, North West Shelf)
Labor relations at major LNG processing plants
Australian Domestic Gas Security Mechanism (ADGSM), which can restrict exports to protect domestic supply
paths.why_it_matters: Australia is one of the world's two or three largest LNG exporters in most years (alongside the United States and Qatar), and its exports go almost entirely to Northeast Asian buyers -- primarily China, Japan, and South Korea. Unlike Gulf Coast or Persian Gulf LNG, most Australian cargoes reach Asian buyers via open ocean without transiting a narrow strait, so the route's main vulnerabilities are concentrated further upstream: a small number of large processing hubs in Western Australia, labor disputes at those plants, and Australia's own domestic-gas-security policy, any of which can move global LNG prices given Australia's outsized share of world supply.
historical_precedents: Australia's LNG export capacity grew from 2.6 billion cubic feet per day in 2011 to more than 11.4 Bcf/d by 2019 as eight new liquefaction projects (including Gorgon, Wheatstone, Ichthys, and the Prelude floating LNG facility) came online, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In September 2023, the Offshore Alliance union group staged rolling strikes at Chevron's Gorgon and Wheatstone LNG plants, which together account for about 7% of global LNG supply; fears of a prolonged shutdown pushed European gas prices higher before the dispute was resolved later that month.
paths.estimated_global_share: Australia, alongside the United States and Qatar, was one of the world's three largest LNG exporters, with the trio together accounting for 63% of global LNG exports in 2025 (up from 60% in 2024); Australia's exports have ranged between 10.2 and 10.7 billion cubic feet per day annually since 2020, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Colonial Pipeline U.S. East Coast Refined Products Corridor
chokepoints: Colonial Pipeline (single 5,500-mile pipeline system)
paths.why_it_matters: The Colonial Pipeline is the largest-capacity refined-products pipeline system in the United States, moving gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and heating oil about 5,500 miles from Gulf Coast refineries in Houston, Texas, to the Mid-Atlantic, Southeast, and as far north as Linden, New Jersey. Because the pipeline is effectively the sole large-volume link between Gulf Coast refining capacity and East Coast demand, with no comparable-capacity alternative, even localized outages -- whether from a physical leak or a cybersecurity incident -- can quickly cause regional fuel shortages, panic buying, and localized price spikes across a dozen or more states.
historical_precedents: On September 9, 2016, a leak was discovered on Colonial's Line 1 in Shelby County, Alabama; the resulting shutdown of the line, which normally carries about 1.4 million barrels per day of gasoline, disrupted supply to five states (Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia) representing about 12% of total U.S. gasoline consumption, and pushed regional retail gasoline prices up about 8 cents per gallon in the following days, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

On May 7, 2021, Colonial Pipeline shut down its entire system for six days after a ransomware attack on its business network; the shutdown, combined with panic buying at retail stations across more than a dozen states, pushed the U.S. average retail gasoline price above $3.00 per gallon for the first time since 2014 and prompted a federal emergency declaration, even though EIA-affiliated research later estimated the shutdown itself directly added only a few cents per gallon to regional prices.
paths.estimated_global_share: Colonial Pipeline is a 2.5-million-barrel-per-day system spanning approximately 5,500 miles, making it the largest-capacity refined-products pipeline in the United States and, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration, a significant mode of transportation-fuel shipment for the East Coast.

paths.name: Global Helium Extraction and Cryogenic Export Network
origin_regions: United States (Texas, Kansas, and other Great Plains and Rocky Mountain natural-gas fields)
chokepoints: Cliffside Field/Bush Dome helium storage reservoir and BLM Pipeline & Storage System near Amarillo, Texas (privatized to Messer in 2024)
Ras Laffan Industrial City liquefaction and export terminal, Qatar
Arzew helium liquefaction plant (Helios joint venture), Algeria
Gazprom's Amur Gas Processing Plant and Primorsky Region export hub near Vladivostok, Russia
Specialized ISO cryogenic liquid-helium container shipping (no dedicated international helium pipeline network)
destination_regions: United States (semiconductor fabrication and MRI manufacturing)
East Asia (China, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan)
paths.why_it_matters: Helium is not manufactured but recovered only as a minor byproduct of a small number of natural-gas fields concentrated enough in helium to justify separation, and it has no substitute for many uses, including cooling the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners and semiconductor lithography tools, so the market is unusually exposed to single-facility outages. The United States privatized its century-old Federal Helium Reserve in Amarillo, Texas -- long the world's largest strategic helium stockpile -- selling the system to Messer for $460 million in a sale completed in June 2024, ending direct federal control just as global supply growth has come to depend on a handful of newer plants in Russia and Canada. With only about five companies controlling most of the world's helium liquefaction and distribution and no international pipeline network, even modest supply losses have repeatedly caused multi-year global shortages and price spikes of 50% or more for end users, per USGS and industry reporting.
historical_precedents: In November 2017, a regional diplomatic and trade dispute closed Qatar's only overland export route, forcing RasGas to shut down its two Ras Laffan helium plants -- then supplying about 25% of world helium demand -- while an industry consultant warned that a disruption lasting more than a month could double global helium prices based on prior shortage episodes, per Gulf News.

A fire on 8 October 2021 and a further explosion on 5 January 2022 at natural-gas processing units feeding Gazprom's new Amur helium complex delayed its planned 60-million-cubic-meter-per-year output, and combined with a January-June 2022 outage of the U.S. Bureau of Land Management's Crude Helium Enrichment Unit that removed more than 10% of global capacity, contributed to 'Helium Shortage 4.0,' during which four of the world's five major helium suppliers declared force majeure and prices rose 50-100% for most users, per Kornbluth Helium Consulting (Innovation News Network) and Chemical & Engineering News.
paths.estimated_global_share: The United States produced an estimated 81 million cubic meters of helium in 2025 (about 43% of an estimated 190 million cubic meter world total), followed by Qatar at 63 million cubic meters (about 33%), Russia at 18 million cubic meters (about 9%), Algeria at 11 million cubic meters (about 6%), and Canada at 6 million cubic meters (about 3%). The United States also held an estimated 8.5 billion cubic meters of identified helium reserves, more than four times Algeria's 1.8 billion and Russia's 1.7 billion cubic meters, per the U.S. Geological Survey Mineral Commodity Summaries (2026).

paths.name: Titanium Dioxide Pigment and Ilmenite/Rutile Ore Supply Chain
origin_regions: China (Sichuan, Yunnan, Guangxi, Hainan mineral sands and slag/pigment plants)
chokepoints: TiO2 pigment manufacturing capacity concentrated in China, which held roughly 56% of world nameplate pigment capacity at year-end 2024 (5.5 of 9.8 million tons), per USGS

Feedstock-grade bottleneck: chloride-process pigment plants require high-titanium rutile, synthetic rutile, or slag, sourced from a small number of mines and upgraders, while ilmenite (about 90% of world titanium-mineral consumption) mainly feeds the sulfate process
Mineral-sands mines are geographically concentrated and vulnerable to localized security or community disruptions, as at South Africa's Richards Bay Minerals
A widening set of national antidumping duties on Chinese TiO2 exports (EU, Brazil, Eurasian Economic Union) is fragmenting what had been a globally integrated pigment trade flow

paths.why_it_matters: Titanium dioxide is the world's dominant white pigment, with U.S. producers alone valuing 2024 output at an estimated $3 billion and consuming more than 95% of domestically available titanium mineral concentrates for paint, plastics, and paper applications, per USGS. Because ore mining is concentrated in a handful of countries and pigment manufacturing capacity is now more than half based in China, localized mine disruptions or shifts in Chinese export and trade-defense policy can move global pigment availability and prices for downstream coatings, plastics, and paper industries worldwide.
historical_precedents: Rio Tinto's Richards Bay Minerals (South Africa) declared force majeure on customer contracts on June 30, 2021, and by July 21, 2021 had shut one of its four furnaces after mining was halted due to an escalating security situation that depleted the feedstock stockpile, curtailing output at one of the world's largest ilmenite/rutile/zircon mineral-sands operations, per Rio Tinto's own press release. A separate, earlier halt to RBM's R6.5-billion Zulti South mine extension in December 2019 was projected to cost South Africa R100 billion in benefits over 25 years, per Engineering News.

The European Commission imposed definitive antidumping duties of €0.25 to €0.74 per kilogram on titanium dioxide imports from China effective January 9, 2025 (following provisional duties in July 2024), finding Chinese imports were being dumped and damaging an EU industry employing almost 5,000 people; Brazil, India, and the Eurasian Economic Union opened or imposed parallel measures (Brazil's ranging from $578 to $1,421 per ton, the EAEU's up to 16.25%), together affecting an estimated 650,000 of China's 1.65 million tons of 2023 TiO2 exports, per the European Commission and PCI Magazine.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for about one-third of global ilmenite mine production in 2024 (3.3 of 8.9 million tons, roughly 37%), with Mozambique (1.9 million tons, ~21%) and South Africa (1.3 million tons, ~15%) the next-largest producers; Australia, Canada, Norway, Senegal, and Madagascar round out the remaining supply. On the pigment side, China held an estimated 56% of world TiO2 pigment nameplate capacity (5.5 of 9.8 million tons) at year-end 2024, versus about 14% for the United States, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025.

paths.name: Neon Gas for Semiconductor Lithography
origin_regions: Russia (crude neon feedstock from steel-industry air separation)
China (steel-mill air separation units; growing purification capacity)
United States (Gulf Coast facility, e.g. Linde's Texas neon plant)
chokepoints: Concentration of semiconductor-grade neon purification capacity in a small number of Ukrainian refiners (Ingas, Cryoin, Iceblick) prior to 2022
Structural dependence of neon supply on byproduct output from large-scale steel-mill oxygen (cryogenic air-separation) operations, since standalone neon production is generally uneconomical
Limited number of facilities worldwide able to purify crude neon to the 99.999% grade required for the argon-fluoride excimer lasers used in deep ultraviolet photolithography
paths.why_it_matters: Semiconductor-grade neon is a purified byproduct of large-scale steel manufacturing: cryogenic air-separation units that supply oxygen to steel mills recover trace neon (roughly 1 part per 65,000 of air) as a byproduct, which is why standalone neon production is generally uneconomical. Before 2022, more than half of the world's neon purification capacity sat with a small number of refiners in Ukraine, which upgraded crude neon to the 99.999%-pure grade needed for the excimer lasers used in deep ultraviolet chip lithography. A 2022 disruption to steel production and air-separation operations in Ukraine removed an estimated 45-54% of global semiconductor-grade neon supply almost overnight, driving spot prices up roughly eightfold to tenfold within weeks and pushing chipmakers to accelerate sourcing diversification toward China, South Korea, Taiwan, and the United States.
historical_precedents: Beginning in February 2022, a major disruption to steel production and associated air-separation operations in Ukraine halted output at the country's two leading neon refiners, Ingas and Cryoin, which together had supplied an estimated 45% to 54% of the world's semiconductor-grade neon, per Reuters calculations reported by the South China Morning Post (via Yahoo Finance).

Wholesale industrial-grade neon prices in China rose from about 1,850 yuan per cubic metre on February 24, 2022 to roughly 16,000 yuan (about US$2,500) per cubic metre within weeks, an approximately ninefold increase, per the South China Morning Post; SPIE's Photonics Focus separately reported that Chinese neon prices rose roughly tenfold by March 2022 and that Japanese krypton prices rose from $1.72 to $8.60 per liter by January 2023.

In response to the 2022 supply shock, semiconductor-producing economies pursued diversification: South Korea brought a domestic neon purification facility online in late 2022 alongside a recycling program covering an estimated 40% of fab demand, and Taiwan began installing purification systems at blast-furnace air-separation units targeting full local supply by 2025, per SFA (Oxford) market research.
paths.estimated_global_share: Ukraine accounted for an estimated 50-70% of global neon production and about 40% of global krypton production before 2022, with two Ukrainian refiners (Ingas and Cryoin) alone supplying 45-54% of the world's semiconductor-grade neon, per Reuters figures cited by the South China Morning Post and SPIE's Photonics Focus. Following the 2022 disruption, an industry analyst projected China's share of global neon supply could rise from roughly 30% to 50% as buyers diversified, while SFA (Oxford) research estimated China separately operates more than 40% of global air-separation-unit capacity, per the South China Morning Post and SFA (Oxford).

paths.name: China's Fluorspar-to-Fluorochemical (HFC Refrigerant) Supply Chain
origin_regions: China (national fluorspar mining base and fluorochemical/HFC manufacturing clusters led by Juhua, Sinochem, Sanmei, and Dongyue)
chokepoints: Single-country concentration of fluorspar mining and integrated HF-to-HFC processing inside China (about 62% of world mine output in 2024)
Chinese Ministry of Natural Resources/Mine Safety Administration nationwide mine-safety inspection and consolidation campaigns that can halt fluorspar mining across the country
Kigali Amendment-mandated Chinese government quota and licensing system governing HFC production facilities and every import/export shipment
Limited non-Chinese HF, HFC, and fluoropolymer processing capacity as producers elsewhere scale back under the same global HFC phasedown
destination_regions: Japan and South Korea (semiconductor and EV supply chains)
paths.why_it_matters: China mines roughly six in ten tonnes of the world's fluorspar, the essential feedstock for hydrofluoric acid, and uses that HF to manufacture the large majority of the world's HFC refrigerants, fluoropolymers such as PTFE, and related fluorochemicals used in air conditioning, EV batteries, and semiconductor manufacturing. Because this chain is vertically integrated inside China from mine to finished refrigerant gas, Chinese mine-safety campaigns, export-quota decisions, and Kigali Amendment compliance choices can move both raw fluorspar prices and finished refrigerant/fluoropolymer costs worldwide.
historical_precedents: From March through August 2024, China's Ministry of Natural Resources and Mine Safety Administration conducted the country's first-ever nationwide fluorspar mine safety inspection and consolidation campaign, halting operations at many mines; the disruption pushed China's fluorspar imports up 55% in the first half of 2024 (mainly from Mongolia) and lifted FOB China acid-grade fluorspar prices to $540-590 per tonne by mid-March 2024, per the U.S. Geological Survey and Fastmarkets.

2024 was designated the Kigali Amendment 'freeze year' for China: its Ministry of Ecology and Environment capped national HFC production and domestic-use quotas at 1.449 billion and 643 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent respectively and required government licensing for every HFC import and export shipment (nearly 30,000 approvals issued annually since China accepted the Amendment in 2021), formally subjecting the world's largest HFC producer and exporter to binding international supply limits for the first time, per China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment (published via UNEP).
paths.estimated_global_share: China mined an estimated 6.0 million of the world's 10.3 million tonnes of fluorspar in 2024 (about 58% of global mine output, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026's finalized figures, revised from an initial 62% estimate) and holds roughly 110 million of the world's 330 million tonnes of fluorspar reserves (about 33%, also revised upward from an initial 27% estimate based on new government reports), per the U.S. Geological Survey. China is also described as the world's leading producer of HFC refrigerants and accounted for 68% of global HCFC-22 (a key fluorochemical precursor) production, while its HFC emissions alone represented more than 20% of the world's total in 2022, per the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA).

paths.name: West Africa Cocoa Export Corridor
origin_regions: Cote d'Ivoire cocoa-growing regions (Western and Southwestern producing zones)
Ghana cocoa-growing regions (Ashanti, Western, and Bono areas)
chokepoints: Port of Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire
Port of San Pedro, Cote d'Ivoire

destination_regions: European Union (particularly the Netherlands and Belgium)
paths.why_it_matters: Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana together supply well over 60 percent of the world's cocoa beans, the primary raw material for chocolate, confectionery, and cosmetics manufacturing worldwide. Because global cocoa supply is this concentrated in two adjacent West African countries and grown mostly by more than a million small-scale farmers, weather shocks or crop disease in this corridor have outsized effects on world cocoa prices, chocolate manufacturers' costs, and the incomes of West African farming households.
historical_precedents: Heavy rainfall in September-October 2024 and preceding seasons spread brown rot (Phytophthora megakarya) in Cote d'Ivoire and black pod disease in Ghana; Cote d'Ivoire's cocoa bean production fell to 1.76 million metric tons in market year 2023/2024, down from 2.3 million metric tons in 2022/2023 (a roughly 24 percent decline), while Ghana's production fell to 531,000 metric tons in 2023/2024 from 655,808 metric tons the prior season, according to USDA Foreign Agricultural Service GAIN reports on both countries.

The resulting global supply shortfall pushed cocoa futures prices to record nominal highs, more than doubling since August 2023 and reaching over $9,600 per metric ton by March 2024 according to IFPRI analysis; USDA GAIN reporting on Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana subsequently recorded futures near $10,092 per metric ton in December 2024 and as high as roughly $12,000 per metric ton during the 2024 holiday season, before easing toward $8,000 per metric ton in early 2025 as West African weather conditions improved.
paths.estimated_global_share: Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana together account for over 60 percent of global cocoa bean production, with Cote d'Ivoire alone producing roughly one-third of the world total, according to USDA Foreign Agricultural Service GAIN reports on both countries (2025).

paths.name: Indonesia-Malaysia Palm Oil Export Corridor
origin_regions: Peninsular Malaysia and Malaysian Borneo (Sabah and Sarawak)
chokepoints: Port of Belawan, North Sumatra
Port of Dumai, Riau
Strait of Malacca shipping lanes
Port Klang, Malaysia
paths.why_it_matters: Indonesia and Malaysia together supply about 85 percent of the world's palm oil, the most widely produced and consumed vegetable oil, used in roughly half of packaged supermarket products as well as in cosmetics and biofuel. Because palm oil meets an estimated 40 percent of global vegetable-oil demand from a small fraction of the land used to grow oil crops, and because supply is so concentrated in these two neighboring countries, domestic policy changes there -- export restrictions, biodiesel blending mandates, or weather-driven production shifts -- quickly transmit to cooking-oil prices in price-sensitive import markets such as India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh.
historical_precedents: Indonesia imposed a full ban on palm oil exports from April 28 to May 23, 2022, to address a domestic cooking-oil shortage; the restriction contributed to a 7 percent rise in palm oil prices that April alone, part of a broader 30 percent surge in global vegetable oil prices since February 2022, according to USDA Foreign Agricultural Service data cited in an IISD/State of Sustainability Initiatives global market report.

Indonesia's Domestic Market Obligation policy, tightened to secure domestic cooking-oil supplies ahead of Ramadan and Eid festivities between February and May 2023, led USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service to revise Indonesia's 2022/23 palm oil export forecast down to 28.4 million metric tons; Indonesia's palm oil exports for October 2022-January 2023 nonetheless reached 10.7 million metric tons, 46 percent higher than the same period a year earlier, as the policy was subsequently relaxed.
paths.estimated_global_share: Indonesia, Malaysia, and Guatemala have been the largest palm oil exporting countries since 2016, shipping 25.5 million metric tons, 13.5 million metric tons, and 0.8 million metric tons respectively in 2021; together Indonesia and Malaysia supply about 85 percent of global palm oil production, according to FAO data cited in an IISD/State of Sustainability Initiatives global market report (June 2023). USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service separately forecasts Indonesian palm oil production at 46 million metric tons and exports at 28.5 million metric tons for market year 2023/24, and Malaysian production at 19.85 million metric tons and exports at 15.9 million metric tons for market year 2026/27.

paths.why_it_matters: The United States and Brazil together export more raw cotton than the rest of the world combined, supplying the fiber that feeds textile and garment manufacturing hubs across South and East Asia. Because global apparel supply chains depend on a small number of exporting countries for a raw input with no ready substitute in cotton-based textiles, weather, competitiveness shifts, or trade-policy changes affecting the US or Brazilian crop quickly transmit to textile-manufacturing costs in Bangladesh, Vietnam, and China, and from there to global apparel prices.

paths.why_it_matters: Titanium alloys make up roughly 14-15% of the airframe weight of modern widebody jets such as the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350, prized for their strength-to-weight ratio and corrosion resistance, and qualifying a new aerospace-grade titanium supplier is a multi-year process due to strict certification requirements. For decades this left Boeing and Airbus each sourcing a majority of their titanium from a single supplier, Russia's VSMPO-AVISMA, creating a concentrated single-source dependency in an industry where switching suppliers cannot happen quickly, regardless of price or politics.
historical_precedents: Following sanctions and a wave of corporate exits from Russia after February 2022, Boeing halted purchases of Russian titanium in March 2022, while Airbus continued sourcing from VSMPO-AVISMA for longer before gradually diversifying to roughly 20% of its titanium needs from Russia; both companies and their suppliers had to qualify additional titanium sources in the U.S., Japan, and elsewhere, a process industry reporting described as taking years given aerospace certification requirements.

Embraer reduced its reliance on VSMPO-AVISMA from about 85% to about 60% of its titanium needs in the years following 2022, illustrating the multi-year pace at which even a mid-sized aircraft manufacturer can diversify a concentrated titanium supply chain.
paths.estimated_global_share: Boeing reportedly sourced as much as 80% of its titanium from Russia's VSMPO-AVISMA before 2022, and Airbus an estimated up to 60%, per industry reporting. chokepoints: Single-country mine-supply concentration in China, which produced an estimated 83% of world mine output in 2024

paths.why_it_matters: Tungsten's extreme hardness, density, and high melting point make it essential to cemented-carbide cutting and mining tools, armor-piercing ammunition, and high-density aerospace components, and USGS notes that most substitutes only reduce rather than replace the amount of tungsten used. China both mines the large majority of the world's tungsten and dominates the refining of ore into ammonium paratungstate (APT) and tungsten carbide, the intermediate products downstream toolmakers and defense manufacturers actually consume. Since 2025, Beijing has layered licensing requirements and then a firm-specific export whitelist onto tungsten trade, giving it fine-grained control over which countries and companies receive supply -- a lever already used narrowly against Japan and one that could be extended to other buyers.
historical_precedents: In September 2024, the U.S. Trade Representative announced a Section 301 tariff increase of 25% on imports of tungsten carbides, concentrates, oxides, powders, and tungstates from China, reflecting concern about U.S. reliance on Chinese tungsten supply, per USGS.

Beginning in February 2025, China required export licenses for tungsten and four other minerals (tellurium, bismuth, molybdenum, and indium); Chinese exports of ammonium paratungstate fell by roughly 70%, from 782 tonnes in 2024 to about 243 tonnes in January-November 2025, and in December 2025 China said it would restrict 2026-2027 tungsten exports to 15 licensed companies.

In January 2026, China's Ministry of Commerce imposed additional export restrictions on dual-use tungsten products destined for Japan; Chinese producers subsequently halted ammonium paratungstate shipments to Japan entirely, though traders noted Japanese buyers could partly substitute supply from Vietnam.

paths.why_it_matters: Tin solder joins the large majority of the world's circuit boards and electronic components, accounting for roughly half of global tin demand, with only partial substitutes such as epoxy resins available for narrower applications. Indonesia is the world's second-largest tin producer, and its export licensing, exchange-based trading rules, and downstream-processing requirements can move global prices, while much of the remaining supply comes from a small number of countries -- China, Myanmar, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo -- where mining is at times artisanal and subject to abrupt suspension. paths.name: Manganese: South Africa and Gabon's Grip on Steelmaking Supply
origin_regions: Australia, Brazil, Ghana, and Cote d'Ivoire (secondary producing regions)
chokepoints: Combined mine-supply concentration: South Africa and Gabon together accounted for an estimated 60% of 2024 world manganese-content mine production
No satisfactory substitute exists for manganese in its primary steelmaking role, per USGS, leaving steelmakers unable to switch inputs during a supply disruption

Processing of manganese ore into the ferromanganese and silicomanganese ferroalloys steelmakers actually use is itself concentrated among a handful of countries; Malaysia, Australia, Norway, and South Africa together supplied more than two-thirds of U.S. ferromanganese imports in 2020-23, per USGS
destination_regions: Global steel-producing regions, including East Asia, Europe, and North America

paths.why_it_matters: Manganese is an essential steelmaking input, used for its sulfur-fixing, deoxidizing, and alloying properties, and the U.S. Geological Survey states it has no satisfactory substitute in its major applications -- steel producers cannot simply switch to another element if supply tightens. South Africa and Gabon together supply roughly three-fifths of the world's mined manganese, and South Africa alone holds an estimated 70% of world manganese resources, so disruptions to mining or transport in either country can ripple through global steel costs. A second concentration point sits downstream, where a small number of countries process raw ore into the ferromanganese and silicomanganese alloys that steel mills actually consume.
historical_precedents: In 2020, COVID-19 lockdowns temporarily halted manganese mining and shipping operations in South Africa; ore prices rose toward multi-year highs on supply concerns before easing as South African and Gabonese output resumed later in the year.

Since late 2023, at least two manganese mining and processing operations in Ukraine, historically a mid-sized global supplier, have remained largely idle, with two others resuming only minimal production by mid-2024, according to USGS -- illustrating how quickly a single-country disruption can remove supply from the global market.

In May 2024, the European Union's Critical Raw Materials Act entered into force, designating high-purity (battery-grade) manganese as a strategic raw material and manganese overall as a critical raw material, reflecting concern about the concentration of supply among a small number of producing countries.

paths.name: Japan's Dominance in Geothermal Steam Turbine Manufacturing
chokepoints: Three Japanese manufacturers, Fuji Electric, Mitsubishi Power, and Toshiba, have supplied a combined majority of the world's geothermal steam turbines for decades

paths.why_it_matters: Utility-scale geothermal power plants depend on a small number of manufacturers capable of building large steam turbines that can withstand corrosive, mineral-laden geothermal fluids, and that capability has been concentrated in Japan for decades. Fuji Electric says it has held the world's largest share of geothermal steam turbine orders, 36%, since 2000, having supplied 84 units totaling 3,469 MW worldwide, while Toshiba says it has delivered more than 3.7 GW of geothermal steam turbines since 1966. The concentration is reinforced by financing structure: large geothermal projects in developing countries are often built with Japanese government ODA loans administered by JICA, which have frequently been paired with contracts for Japanese-manufactured turbines, tying project financing to equipment sourcing in a way that is unusual among renewable-energy equipment categories.
historical_precedents: Fuji Electric states on its corporate website that it has received orders in Japan and overseas for 84 units of geothermal steam turbine power-generation equipment (9 of them in Japan) totaling 3,469 MW, giving it the world's largest share of orders, 36%, of any manufacturer since 2000.

Kenya's 86.2 MW Olkaria V geothermal unit, financed through an ODA loan the Japanese government extended to Kenya Electricity Generating Company (KenGen) via JICA, began commercial operation in December 2019 with its steam turbine, generator, and condenser supplied by Mitsubishi Power, illustrating how Japanese development financing for African geothermal projects has been paired with Japanese-manufactured turbine-supply contracts.

paths.why_it_matters: New Zealand is the world's largest dairy exporter on a single-country basis even though it is only the world's seventh-largest producer of cow's milk, because roughly 95 percent of its milk production is exported rather than consumed domestically. Dairy exports were valued at NZ$23.8 billion (US$13.8 billion) in 2024, representing 34 percent of New Zealand's total merchandise exports, and the farmer-owned cooperative Fonterra alone handles about 77 percent of the country's national milk production, giving a single company and a small, weather-exposed pasture-based farm base outsized influence over global dairy commodity prices set on the Global Dairy Trade auction platform.

USDA's FAS Wellington post reported in November 2025 that Earth Sciences New Zealand (formerly NIWA) put the likelihood of La Nina conditions developing before the end of 2025 at around 60 percent, a factor it flagged as a key swing input for 2026 pasture growth and milk output, illustrating how weather in a single small, pasture-dependent country can move a supply base that much of the world's traded dairy relies on.

paths.why_it_matters: Ecuador is the world's largest banana exporter, shipping to more than 70 countries and accounting for roughly a quarter to a third of global banana export volume out of a world export market of around 19-20 million tonnes a year. Nearly all internationally traded bananas are a single variety, the Cavendish, grown as a genetic monoculture with no commercially available disease-resistant replacement, so a disease outbreak in the top exporting country carries outsized risk for global supply, prices, and the roughly 400 million people in producing countries who depend on the crop for food and nutrition security.

In 2022, Ecuadorian banana producers with heavy exposure to Russia and Ukraine as destination markets lost access to shipments after major container lines suspended cargo bookings to and from Russia amid international transport sanctions, leaving exporters with a backlog of unsold fruit that caused oversupply and depressed world banana export prices on multiple occasions during the year, according to FAO reporting cited in an IISD Global Market Report on bananas.

paths.name: Global Uranium Mining and Enrichment Supply Chain for Nuclear Fuel
origin_regions: United Kingdom and Netherlands (enrichment, via URENCO)
chokepoints: Concentration of primary mine production in Kazakhstan

Concentration of global enrichment capacity among a handful of state-linked enrichment plants (Rosatom/TENEX in Russia, Orano in France, URENCO across the UK/Netherlands/Germany, and Centrus/URENCO USA in the United States)
paths.why_it_matters: Nuclear power plants cannot use mined uranium directly: after mining, uranium must be converted to uranium hexafluoride and enriched, a specialized industrial process concentrated among a small number of state-linked or quasi-state enrichment plants worldwide. This creates two distinct bottlenecks stacked on top of each other -- mine-supply concentration in Kazakhstan, which mines roughly two-fifths of the world's uranium, and enrichment-service concentration among Russia, France, the UK/Netherlands (URENCO), and the United States. Because Russia's Rosatom/TENEX has remained a large supplier of enrichment services to Western utilities even as other Russian energy exports have been restricted, the fuel cycle's processing stage -- not a shipping lane -- is this route's principal vulnerability, and it is a different risk profile from every maritime or overland transport chokepoint elsewhere in this dataset.
historical_precedents: A 2007 fire at a sulfuric acid processing plant supplying Kazakhstan's in-situ-leach uranium mines forced acid rationing that lasted until mid-2008, constraining the country's uranium output well into 2009 -- illustrating how a single input-material bottleneck can ripple through the world's largest uranium-mining base, since in-situ-leach mining requires large volumes of acid to dissolve uranium from ore, per the World Nuclear Association.

Kazakhstan's share of global uranium mine production rose from about 28% in 2009, when it first became the world's leading producer, to roughly 40% in 2025, concentrating primary supply increasingly in a single country even as global reactor fuel demand has grown, per the World Nuclear Association.
paths.estimated_global_share: Kazakhstan supplied about 40% of the world's mined uranium in 2025 and 28% of uranium delivered to U.S. buyers that year (behind Canada's 32%); Russia supplied 26% of the foreign-origin enrichment services (separative work units) purchased by U.S. nuclear utility owners and operators in 2025, out of a foreign-origin share that made up 77% of the 13 million SWU purchased in total that year, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Uranium Marketing Annual Report and the World Nuclear Association.

paths.name: Druzhba Pipeline Russia-to-Europe Crude Oil Corridor
origin_regions: Russia (Volga-Urals oil fields, via Samara and Almetyevsk)
chokepoints: Druzhba Pipeline (Mozyr junction in Belarus, splitting northern and southern branches)
Southern-branch transit across Ukraine
EU country-specific import exemptions
paths.why_it_matters: Druzhba ("Friendship") is one of the world's longest oil pipeline systems, running roughly 5,100 kilometers from Russia's Volga-Urals fields to refineries across Central Europe, and for decades it was the primary route by which several landlocked Central European refineries -- with no direct seaport access for large-scale crude imports -- received crude oil. Unlike the tanker chokepoints elsewhere in this dataset, its main vulnerability is geopolitical and infrastructural rather than navigational: since a 2022 EU restriction on most seaborne Russian crude, paired with a country-specific exemption for pipeline deliveries to landlocked Hungary, Slovakia, and (until 2025) Czechia, the pipeline's northern branch to Poland and Germany has gone essentially unused, while its southern branch, which crosses Ukraine, remains the last significant piped Russian crude route into the EU and is exposed to disruption of the physical infrastructure along that route.
historical_precedents: Following EU restrictions on most Russian seaborne crude oil imports that took effect in December 2022, pipeline deliveries via Druzhba subject to the measures fell from about 1.2 million barrels per day to under 200 thousand barrels per day; Poland and Germany, which voluntarily ended their Druzhba imports, saw northern-branch deliveries cease entirely by early 2023, with Kazakh crude subsequently routed through the same pipeline infrastructure to partly replace the lost volumes reaching German refineries, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In January 2026, the pipeline's infrastructure in western Ukraine sustained damage that halted southern-branch deliveries to Hungary and Slovakia for several months; pumping through the Ukrainian section resumed on April 22, 2026, with the first post-restart cargoes reaching Hungary and Slovakia within a day, illustrating the corridor's continued exposure to disruption along its overland route.
paths.estimated_global_share: Druzhba's combined branches have a nominal capacity of roughly 1.2-1.4 million barrels per day (up to about 2 million barrels per day at full build-out), but deliveries subject to EU restrictions fell to under 200 thousand barrels per day after December 2022, and only the southern branch supplying Hungary and Slovakia was still operating under an EU exemption as of mid-2026, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration and Global Energy Monitor.

paths.name: Enbridge Mainline Canada-to-U.S. Crude Oil Pipeline Network
origin_regions: Canada (Alberta oil sands and Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin, via Edmonton)
chokepoints: Enbridge Mainline pipeline system (Canadian Mainline plus the connecting U.S. Lakehead System)
Border crossing near Gretna, Manitoba
destination_regions: United States Midwest (Superior, Wisconsin and the Chicago area)
United States Gulf Coast (via connecting pipelines)
paths.why_it_matters: The Enbridge Mainline is the largest crude oil pipeline network linking Canada to the United States, carrying Western Canadian crude and diluted bitumen roughly 7,550 kilometers across the Canada Energy Regulator-regulated Canadian Mainline (which connects onward to the U.S. Lakehead System) from Edmonton, Alberta to refining and distribution hubs in Sarnia, Ontario and the U.S. Midwest. It carries close to 3 million barrels per day and represents about 70% of Western Canada's crude oil export pipeline capacity, making it functionally the single largest artery for Canadian oil; because Canada supplies well over half of total U.S. crude oil imports, almost entirely by pipeline, an outage on the Mainline has an outsized effect on Midwest refinery feedstock costs and on the market value of Canadian heavy crude, which otherwise has few large-volume alternative routes to market.
historical_precedents: On July 26, 2010, a rupture on Enbridge's 30-inch Line 6B near Marshall, Michigan (part of the Mainline's U.S. Lakehead System) spilled hundreds of thousands of gallons of diluted bitumen into Talmadge Creek and the Kalamazoo River; cleanup crews recovered more than 1.2 million gallons of oil and contaminated sediment between 2010 and 2014, and in 2016 Enbridge agreed to spend at least $110 million on measures to prevent future spills and improve operations across nearly 2,000 miles of pipeline in the Great Lakes region, per the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

The Line 3 replacement pipeline, part of the Mainline system, became fully operational on October 1, 2021, raising that single line's capacity to 760,000 barrels per day (roughly double its prior capacity) and materially increasing the Mainline's total takeaway capacity out of Alberta, illustrating how a single expansion or outage on this network can shift North American crude-oil price differentials by hundreds of thousands of barrels per day, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
paths.estimated_global_share: The Enbridge Mainline carries approximately 3 million barrels per day and represents about 70% of Western Canada's crude oil pipeline export capacity; Canada supplied more than 60% of total U.S. crude oil imports in 2020, the large majority moving by pipeline rather than rail, per the Canada Energy Regulator and the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Nigeria Crude Oil Exports and Niger Delta Pipeline Network
origin_regions: Nigeria (Niger Delta onshore and offshore fields)
chokepoints: Onshore Niger Delta pipeline network (including the Trans Niger Pipeline)
Bonny, Forcados, and Escravos export terminals
Exposure of onshore pipelines to theft and sabotage
paths.why_it_matters: Nigeria holds Africa's largest proven crude oil reserves and has long been one of the continent's largest producers, but nearly all of its output must first move through a dense onshore pipeline network across the swamps and creeks of the Niger Delta before reaching a small number of coastal export terminals such as Bonny, Forcados, and Escravos. That onshore network -- unlike a maritime strait -- is vulnerable to theft (illegal taps used to divert crude to informal local refineries) and sabotage at thousands of points along its length, which is far harder to secure than a single chokepoint; the resulting production swings have repeatedly forced operators to declare force majeure on specific pipelines and terminals, cutting Nigeria's exports even when global oil prices and international demand are favorable.
historical_precedents: Nigeria's crude oil production (excluding lease condensate) briefly fell below 1 million barrels per day in the third quarter of 2022 because of extended disruptions from crude oil theft and pipeline vandalism, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In April 2023, the pipeline operator reported detecting and removing 460 illegal connections used to tap crude oil from the Trans Niger Pipeline before resuming operations, and in March 2025 an explosion on the pipeline put an estimated 450,000 barrels per day of production at risk before operations were restored by rerouting crude to alternative infrastructure.
paths.estimated_global_share: Nigeria held an estimated 37.5 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves in 2024, the largest in Africa, but production fell 31% between 2015 and 2024 to about 1.5 million barrels per day, with crude oil theft and pipeline vandalism cited by the U.S. Energy Information Administration as a leading cause; Nigeria exported roughly 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and condensate in 2024, with Europe (about 622,000 b/d) and Asia-Pacific (about 276,000 b/d) the largest destination markets.

paths.name: Israel and Jordan Dead Sea Potash Export Corridor
origin_regions: Dead Sea solar evaporation ponds and processing complexes: Sodom, Israel (ICL Dead Sea Works) and Ghor Al Safi, Jordan (Arab Potash Company)
chokepoints: Dead Sea brine evaporation ponds and processing plants operated on both the Israeli and Jordanian shores
Aqaba port and Jordan Industrial Ports Company export terminal, Jordan (Red Sea)
Red Sea, Bab-el-Mandeb, and Suez Canal shipping lanes
paths.why_it_matters: Unlike the underground and solution mines that supply most of the world's potash, Israel's ICL Dead Sea Works and Jordan's Arab Potash Company both extract potassium chloride from the same inland sea, which forms much of the two countries' shared border, by pumping brine into solar evaporation ponds. ICL reports that about 60% of its raw minerals are excavated in Israel and that roughly 90% of its sales are exports reaching customers in more than 60 countries, while Arab Potash Company exports the great majority of its output through a single Red Sea outlet, the Aqaba port terminal managed by Jordan Industrial Ports Company, with India, China, and Malaysia as its largest markets. Because both national industries draw on one shared, geologically unique brine body and Jordan's exports funnel through one port, a disruption to Dead Sea operations, the Aqaba terminal, or Red Sea shipping lanes would remove supply that food-import-dependent buyers in South and East Asia have come to rely on; potassium has no agricultural substitute.
historical_precedents: 2023-2024: Israel's potash production declined from 2.33 million to 2.26 million metric tons even as Jordan's rose from 1.70 million to a finalized 1.73 million metric tons, against a finalized world 2024 total of 46.7 million tons; Jordan's production went on to reach 1.80 million tons in 2025 (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, which revised the 2024 figures from an initial 2025 estimate of Israel 2.40 million / world 48.0 million tons).

2020-2022: The USGS-tracked average potash price (f.o.b. mine, K2O equivalent) rose from about $850 per metric ton in 2020 to about $1,790 per ton in 2022 before easing to roughly $1,220 per ton by 2024, price swings that fed directly into Dead Sea Works' and Arab Potash Company's revenue since both sell into the same world market as Canadian, Russian, and Belarusian producers (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2008-2013: Arab Potash Company and Jordan Phosphate Mines Company formed the joint venture Jordan Industrial Ports Company in 2009 and began implementing a 2008 agreement to refurbish, upgrade, and expand the export jetty at Aqaba, the sole marine outlet for Jordanian potash shipments (Arab Potash Company, via Wikipedia).
paths.estimated_global_share: Israel and Jordan together produced an estimated 3.99 million of the world's 46.7 million metric tons of potash in 2024 (about 9%), with Israel the world's seventh-largest and Jordan the eighth-largest potash-producing country by volume that year (Germany and Laos both now rank above them in USGS's finalized 2024 table); USGS lists both countries' reserves as 'large' rather than a specific figure because both draw on the Dead Sea, which holds nearly 2 billion metric tons of potassium chloride, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026.

paths.name: Germany (K+S AG) Potash Export Network
origin_regions: Werra-Fulda potash mining district, Hesse and Thuringia, Germany (K+S KALI GmbH mines at Unterbreizbach, Wintershall, and Hattorf)
chokepoints: K+S KALI GmbH underground mine and processing complex, Werra-Fulda district, Germany
K+S Transport GmbH rail and shipping logistics network, headquartered in Hamburg, Germany
paths.why_it_matters: Germany's potash industry is concentrated in a single historic mining district straddling Hesse and Thuringia, where K+S AG -- Germany's sole potash producer and, by its own description, Europe's largest supplier of potash for fertilizer use -- operates underground mines that were split by the Cold War-era inner-German border until 1990 reunification restored integrated control and logistics. Output from the district's mines and processing plants moves through a single company's rail and shipping network, run by Hamburg-based K+S Transport GmbH, to K+S's largest confirmed European markets: Belgium, France, Italy, and the Netherlands. Because German potash output is concentrated both in one Zechstein-era salt formation and in a single vertically integrated company's logistics chain, an operational disruption at the Werra-Fulda mines or within K+S's transport network would have an outsized effect on potash supply for Western European farmers, who have fewer nearby alternative suppliers than importers on other continents; potassium has no agricultural substitute.
historical_precedents: 2023-2024: Germany's potash production declined from 2.70 million to a finalized 2.5 million metric tons, not the roughly 11% rise to 3.0 million tons an earlier provisional estimate had shown, though Germany still ranked among the world's top five potash-producing countries that year (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

1990: German reunification ended the Cold War-era division of the Werra-Fulda potash mining district across the inner-German border, which had complicated mining and transport logistics in the region for decades (Werra-Kalirevier, German Wikipedia).

2020-2022: The USGS-tracked average potash price (f.o.b. mine, K2O equivalent) rose from about $850 per metric ton in 2020 to about $1,790 per ton in 2022 before easing to roughly $1,220 per ton by 2024, price swings that applied to K+S as a global price-taker alongside Canadian, Russian, Israeli, Jordanian, and Belarusian producers (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).
paths.estimated_global_share: Germany produced an estimated 2.5 million of the world's 46.7 million metric tons of potash in 2024 (about 5%), and holds roughly 150 million of the world's more than 5.9 billion metric tons of K2O-equivalent potash reserves (about 2.5%), per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (which revised the 2024 production figure down from an initial 3.0 million estimate, and the world reserve total up from 4.8 billion tons a year earlier). K+S AG describes itself as Europe's largest supplier of potash for fertilizer use, with about 51 sites and roughly 11,000 employees across 22 countries (K+S AG, company website).

paths.name: Molybdenum-99/Technetium-99m Medical Isotope Reactor Supply Concentration
commodities: technetium-99m (Tc-99m) generators for diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging
origin_regions: Czech Republic and Poland (LVR-15 and Maria research reactors)
chokepoints: Almost all world Mo-99 supply is produced by a small number of aging, government-owned research reactors, none of which are located in the United States, the world's largest consumer
Mo-99 has a 66-hour half-life and its decay product Tc-99m has only a 6-hour half-life, so neither can be stockpiled and both must be produced and shipped continuously
The United States had no domestic Mo-99 production capacity as of 2025, relying entirely on imports from overseas reactors nearing the end of their operating licenses
Simultaneous scheduled and unscheduled outages at just two of the small number of producing reactors can trigger a global shortage, as occurred in 2009-2010 and again in 2024
destination_regions: global hospital nuclear medicine and radiology departments
paths.why_it_matters: Technetium-99m, generated from molybdenum-99, is used in an estimated 40,000 nuclear medicine procedures per day in the United States alone - including cardiac stress tests and cancer imaging - according to a September 2025 U.S. Department of Energy National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) update. A 2016 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine study found that just seven research reactors, located in Australia, Belgium, Canada, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, and South Africa, produced over 95% of the Mo-99 used globally for medical purposes. Because Mo-99 and Tc-99m decay too quickly to stockpile, and because the United States has never had domestic production capacity despite being the largest consumer, an outage at even one or two of this small handful of aging reactors can immediately reduce the availability of routine diagnostic scans for hospitals worldwide.
historical_precedents: Starting in May 2009, Canada's NRU reactor - then one of the world's largest Mo-99 suppliers - was shut down for about 15 months after a heavy-water leak was discovered, and this outage overlapped with a separate 2010 maintenance shutdown of the Netherlands' HFR reactor; the combined loss of supply from two of the world's few Mo-99-producing reactors forced hospitals in the United States and Canada to ration nuclear medicine scans and delay some cancer and cardiac diagnostic procedures, prompting the National Academies to undertake its 2016 review of global Mo-99 supply resilience.

In 2024, two overseas Mo-99 production reactors went offline simultaneously - one for scheduled maintenance and one unscheduled - triggering a major shortage that reduced technetium-99m availability for U.S. nuclear medicine procedures, according to the September 2025 DOE NNSA update; in response, NNSA committed $32 million toward SHINE Technologies' new Mo-99 production facility in Janesville, Wisconsin (reported about 75% complete as of that update), and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a $10 per-dose add-on payment for domestically produced radiopharmaceuticals effective January 1, 2026, to help establish the first U.S. domestic Mo-99 supply.
paths.estimated_global_share: Seven research reactors - located in Australia, Belgium, Canada, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, and South Africa - supplied over 95% of world molybdenum-99 demand for medical use, per a 2016 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine study; the United States, which uses the Mo-99 decay product technetium-99m in an estimated 40,000 medical imaging procedures per day, had zero domestic Mo-99 production capacity as of 2025 and relied entirely on these overseas reactors, per the U.S. Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration.

paths.name: China-Sourced Surgical Gown Subcontracting and Sterility-Assurance Recall
commodities: AAMI Level 3 and Level 4 sterile surgical isolation gowns
origin_regions: China (Siyang Holymed and its undisclosed subcontracted manufacturing sites)
chokepoints: Reliance on a single overseas supplier's declared manufacturing sites, with limited direct US visibility into that supplier's own undisclosed subcontractors
Bundling of gowns inside pre-packaged sterile 'procedure packs,' so a single component's sterility failure forced recall of entire multi-item surgical kits rather than just the gowns
Thin surge capacity among alternative AAMI Level 3/4 sterile-gown producers able to rapidly absorb a multi-million-unit supply gap
The recall's timing just before the COVID-19 pandemic compounded a separate, simultaneous worldwide surge in PPE demand
destination_regions: international hospitals and surgery centers supplied by Cardinal Health
paths.why_it_matters: In January 2020, Cardinal Health recalled 9.1 million AAMI Level 3 surgical gowns and took field-correction or recall action on 2.9 million procedure packs, after learning in December 2019 that its supplier, Siyang Holymed, had shifted production to unapproved, uncontrolled subcontracted facilities without Cardinal Health's knowledge, making it unable to assure the gowns' sterility. The recall affected 2,897 hospitals, surgery centers, and other facilities worldwide and forced at least one U.S. hospital chain to cancel roughly 200 elective surgeries, illustrating how a single undisclosed subcontracting decision deep in a sterile medical-supply chain - discovered only weeks before COVID-19 triggered a separate, simultaneous global PPE demand surge - can compromise surgical capacity nationwide with little warning.
historical_precedents: On 30 January 2020, Cardinal Health announced the recall of 9.1 million AAMI Level 3 surgical gowns (manufactured between September 2018 and January 2020) and voluntary field actions covering 2.9 million procedure packs - 374,794 subject to correction and 2,518,653 subject to recall - after determining it could not assure the sterility of gowns made at an unregistered subcontractor site used by supplier Siyang Holymed; Cardinal Health terminated its relationship with the supplier and recorded a $96 million charge in its fiscal second quarter of 2020 for inventory write-offs and remediation.

Cardinal Health responded by ramping up production of AAMI Level 4 gowns and working with industry partners and customers to replace affected inventory, even as the recall's timing in early 2020 coincided with the onset of COVID-19-driven global PPE shortages, compounding pressure on hospitals' gown supplies from two independent causes at once.
paths.estimated_global_share: The recalled gowns and affected procedure packs from a single supplier's undisclosed subcontractor reached 2,897 hospitals, surgery centers, and other facilities worldwide, per Cardinal Health; the resulting shortage was severe enough that at least one U.S. hospital chain cancelled about 200 elective surgeries, per contemporaneous healthcare trade press reporting.

paths.name: Global Semiconductor Shortage Impact on Medical Device Manufacturing
commodities: semiconductor chips and microcontrollers used in medical devices
patient monitors and diagnostic imaging electronics
origin_regions: Taiwan, South Korea, and other concentrated global semiconductor fabrication hubs supplying the legacy-node chips used in medical electronics
chokepoints: Medical-device semiconductor demand represented only about 1% of the $415 billion global semiconductor market in 2019 (about $5.1 billion), giving medtech buyers little purchasing priority relative to the much larger automotive and consumer-electronics sectors during a shortage

Over 70% of surveyed medtech companies reported that more than half of their semiconductor components were single-sourced, per AdvaMed, leaving little flexibility to substitute suppliers on short notice
Lengthy FDA regulatory requalification requirements for even minor component substitutions slow a device maker's ability to switch chip suppliers once a shortage begins
paths.why_it_matters: Semiconductors are embedded in the large majority of modern medical devices, from implantable pacemakers to infusion pumps and automated external defibrillators, yet medical-device demand accounted for only about 1% of the $415 billion global semiconductor market in 2019, according to AdvaMed, the medical technology industry association. Because chip foundries prioritize their largest customers, medtech manufacturers found themselves last in line behind automakers and consumer-electronics companies during the 2021-2022 global semiconductor shortage, even though over 70% of surveyed medtech firms reported that more than half of their chip components had no qualified second source. The result was component lead times ranging from two to more than 52 weeks, and the FDA added devices including automated external defibrillators to its medical device shortage list, citing semiconductor supply constraints alongside rising demand.
historical_precedents: Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) were added to the FDA's medical device shortage list in July 2022, with the agency citing both increased demand for the devices and the ongoing global semiconductor shortage as contributing causes, according to trade-press reporting on FDA shortage-list updates.

Infusion pumps made by Fresenius Kabi AG, including its Agilia infusion pump line, were among the devices affected by semiconductor-driven component shortages during the 2021-2022 chip crunch, according to trade-press reporting on FDA medical device shortage list updates; AdvaMed's 2021 industry survey found that all responding medtech companies had experienced some disruption to their chip supply chains.
paths.estimated_global_share: Medical-device semiconductor demand represented only about 1% of the $415 billion global semiconductor market in 2019 (roughly $5.1 billion), per AdvaMed; over 70% of medtech companies surveyed by AdvaMed reported that more than half of their semiconductor components were single-sourced, leaving device makers with little purchasing leverage or substitution flexibility during the 2021-2022 global chip shortage.

paths.name: China's Metallurgical-Grade Silicon Metal and Polysilicon Supply Chain
origin_regions: China (Xinjiang, Yunnan, Sichuan, Inner Mongolia, Fujian)
chokepoints: Single-country concentration of raw silicon metal smelting (China supplies roughly 85% of world output)
Even deeper downstream concentration in polysilicon refining, the further-purified material used in solar wafers and semiconductor chips (China holds over 90% of global capacity)
Energy-intensive carbothermic reduction (quartz plus carbon in an electric-arc furnace) ties output directly to regional electricity availability and cost
destination_regions: global solar photovoltaic module and wafer manufacturers
global silicone/siloxane chemical manufacturers (construction sealants, cosmetics, electronics)
steel and aluminum alloy producers worldwide
paths.why_it_matters: Metallurgical-grade silicon metal, made by reducing quartz with carbon in an electric-arc furnace, is the starting feedstock for two large global chemical value chains: silicone/siloxane chemicals (used in sealants, cosmetics, and electronics) and, after further chemical purification via the Siemens trichlorosilane process, polysilicon, the essential input for solar photovoltaic wafers and semiconductor chips. China does not merely dominate one link of this chain; it dominates both the raw smelting stage and the further-refined polysilicon stage, giving it a depth of concentration across an entire multi-stage industrial chemical supply chain rather than a single mining or refining chokepoint.
historical_precedents: China's share of global polysilicon production capacity rose from near zero in 2004 to 55% in 2018 and to over 90% by 2023, according to Bernreuter Research, a specialist polysilicon market analysis firm; the shift accelerated after a wave of consolidation in which more than 40 polysilicon plants worldwide, most of them in China, shut down between late 2010 and early 2013 amid a global supply glut, followed by the introduction of protectionist Chinese import duties in 2013 that helped entrench sustained Chinese production dominance over foreign competitors.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for approximately 87% of the 5.5 million metric tons of world silicon metal production in 2024 (producing 4.8 million metric tons), per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026's finalized figures -- a materially larger tonnage and share than an earlier estimate of 3.9/4.6 million tons (85%) published a year before; 2025 production was estimated to ease to 4.0 of 4.6 million tons amid oversupply and weak demand. China's share of global polysilicon production capacity, the further-refined material used in solar panels and semiconductor wafers, stood at over 90% as of 2023, up from 55% in 2018 and near zero in 2004, per Bernreuter Research.

paths.name: Global Industrial and Merchant Gas Supply Network (Oxygen, Nitrogen, Argon, Hydrogen)
origin_regions: Linde plc (Ireland/Germany-headquartered, formed from the 2018 Linde AG-Praxair merger)
on-site air separation units built adjacent to individual steel, chemical, refining, and electronics plants worldwide
chokepoints: Oligopoly concentration: Linde plc, Air Liquide, and Air Products and Chemicals are the three largest global suppliers of industrial and merchant gases

The dominant supply model uses dedicated 'on-site' air separation units built next to a single customer's facility and linked by a short pipeline, meaning a plant outage typically has no local backup supplier
High capital cost, cryogenic handling, and pipeline-dependent logistics limit the number of firms able to build and operate this infrastructure at scale
destination_regions: food and beverage, welding, and general manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Global heavy industry depends on a small number of companies that design, build, and operate the air separation units and hydrogen plants supplying oxygen, nitrogen, argon, and hydrogen to steel mills, refineries, chemical plants, semiconductor fabs, and hospitals. Because the most efficient way to serve a large industrial customer is a dedicated on-site plant physically connected to that single customer, most of this supply has no nearby alternate source: if an on-site unit goes down, the host facility must curtail production or arrange trucked-in cryogenic liquid gas at a premium rather than switch suppliers. Decades of consolidation among the largest suppliers, culminating in the 2018 merger that created Linde plc as the world's largest industrial gas company, has further concentrated the specialized capital and engineering expertise needed to build and run this infrastructure.
historical_precedents: Linde AG and Praxair completed their merger to form Linde plc on October 31, 2018, creating the world's largest industrial gas supplier by revenue and market share; to secure antitrust approval, the combined company divested a substantial package of North and South American production assets to Messer Group and CVC Capital Partners for $3.3 billion in July 2018, with the remaining US-required divestitures finalized by March 1, 2019, illustrating how concentrated regulators judged the global industrial gas market to already be even before allowing the merger to proceed.
paths.estimated_global_share: Linde plc, formed by the 2018 merger of Linde AG and Praxair, is the world's largest industrial gas supplier by revenue and market share, reporting US$33.01 billion in revenue in 2024; Air Liquide is the second-largest global supplier by revenue, reporting EUR 27 billion in 2025; and Air Products and Chemicals, the third major global player, reported US$12.04 billion in revenue for fiscal year 2025, according to each company's published financial disclosures.

paths.name: China Shipping Container Manufacturing Concentration
origin_regions: China (Yangtze River Delta and Pearl River Delta container-manufacturing clusters)
chokepoints: Three Chinese manufacturers (CIMC, Dong Fang International Containers, and CXIC Group) controlling the large majority of world container output
Corten (weathering) steel and coating inputs concentrated in the same manufacturing clusters
Minimal spare box-building capacity outside China to absorb a supply disruption or trade restriction
paths.why_it_matters: The steel boxes that carry the large majority of the world's non-bulk seaborne trade are themselves manufactured almost entirely in one country, a distinct chokepoint from the ships that carry them or the canals they transit. Because container-factory capacity is concentrated among just three Chinese producers, a manufacturing disruption, trade restriction, or demand spike in China can tighten the global supply of containers directly, raising freight and leasing costs and constraining how quickly shipping lines can respond to a rebound in trade volumes.
historical_precedents: A post-COVID demand surge combined with 2020-2021 manufacturing and logistics disruptions caused a global shortage of shipping containers; prices for a new dry container rose from roughly $1,650-$1,750 per TEU at the end of 2019 to about $3,500 by the end of 2020, per Drewry data reported by FreightWaves, contributing to the broader 2021 freight-rate spike and port congestion.

In April 2025 the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative announced Section 301 fees on operators of China-built ships tied in part to container capacity, and proposed additional tariffs on China-built cargo-handling equipment, as part of a broader action targeting China's dominance of the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors.
paths.estimated_global_share: Chinese factories manufacture over 96% of the world's dry cargo shipping containers and 100% of refrigerated containers, per UK maritime consultancy Drewry, cited by FreightWaves in 2021; the three largest Chinese producers, CIMC, Dong Fang International Containers, and CXIC Group, controlled about 82% of global container production in Q1 2021 (42%, 26%, and 14% respectively). Production has remained concentrated in China through 2024, with Drewry reporting Q2 2024 dry-freight container output at a record high and full-year 2024 on pace to be the second-highest year on record, per Trans.INFO reporting.

paths.name: Libya's Oil Export Terminal Network and NOC Production
origin_regions: Libya (Sirte Basin and Murzuq Basin oil fields)
chokepoints: Es Sider, Ras Lanuf, Zueitina, and Marsa el Brega export terminals (eastern Libya)
Zawiya and Mellitah export terminals (western Libya)
Sharara oil field and its export pipeline (southwestern Libya)
Political division between Libya's two rival governments, each able to shut in fields or blockade terminals under its control
paths.why_it_matters: Libya holds Africa's largest proved oil reserves and produces a high-quality light, sweet crude that is easy to refine into valuable products, but nearly all of it must move through a small number of coastal export terminals controlled by one of Libya's two rival governments. Because oil and gas exports fund the large majority of government revenue and export earnings, both authorities have repeatedly used shut-ins or blockades of fields, pipelines, and terminals as political leverage, producing large and abrupt swings in national output that are unrelated to global oil demand or prices. Libya sends most of its crude to a concentrated set of European refiners, so terminal-level disruptions tighten a specific slice of the light-sweet crude market that is not easily replaced by other suppliers.
historical_precedents: Libya's crude oil production collapsed from about 1.65 million barrels per day before a 2011 conflict to near zero by mid-2011, and competing authorities and armed groups have repeatedly blockaded pipelines and export terminals as leverage in the years since: three eastern export terminals were blockaded by an armed group from December 2014 to September 2016, and all eastern loading ports plus the Sharara and El Feel oil-field pipelines were blockaded from January to October 2020, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

A dispute over leadership of Libya's Central Bank, combined with the separate closure of the Sharara oil field (partly operated by Spain's Repsol), cut national crude oil production below 600,000 barrels per day by the end of August and through September 2024; output began recovering in early October 2024 after Libya's rival governments reached an agreement on Central Bank leadership and the national oil company lifted force majeure at the affected fields and ports, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
paths.estimated_global_share: Libya held an estimated 48 billion barrels of proved oil reserves at the start of 2024 (3% of the world's total and 41% of Africa's, the continent's largest) and exported about 1 million barrels per day of crude oil and condensate in 2023, up from 930,000 b/d in 2022; Europe took about 78% of Libya's crude oil and condensate exports in 2023 (mainly Italy, Germany, and Spain) and Asia about 10% (mostly China), while crude oil and natural gas exports accounted for an estimated 93% of Libya's total export value and 97% of government revenue that year, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

paths.name: Colombia's Coal Exports from La Guajira and Cesar
origin_regions: Colombia (La Guajira and Cesar departments, including the Cerrejón open-pit mine)
chokepoints: The roughly 150-kilometer private rail line linking the Cerrejón mine to Puerto Bolívar, La Guajira, the sole rail/port evacuation route for the mine's output
Puerto Bolívar, described as the largest coal-export port in Latin America, capable of loading vessels up to 180,000 tonnes

Single-company ownership of Cerrejón, now wholly owned by Glencore after it bought out former co-owners BHP and Anglo American, concentrating a large share of Colombia's coal exports under one operator
Labor relations at Cerrejón and other La Guajira/Cesar mines, where extended strikes have previously cut national coal output sharply
Disputes with local Wayuu indigenous communities over water use and environmental impacts, which have drawn United Nations human-rights scrutiny and periodic calls to halt operations
paths.why_it_matters: Colombia is South America's largest coal producer and exports the great majority of what it mines, since the country relies mainly on hydropower for domestic electricity. Output is concentrated in a small number of large open-pit mines in the La Guajira and Cesar departments in the north of the country, moved by dedicated rail lines to a handful of Caribbean coast export terminals, chief among them Puerto Bolívar, which serves the Cerrejón mine, one of the largest open-pit coal mines in the world. That concentration of production, transport, and ownership (Cerrejón is now wholly owned by Glencore) means a single strike, rail disruption, or community dispute can quickly cut into global seaborne coal supply, and Colombian coal has historically been an important source of U.S. and European coal imports.
historical_precedents: Colombia's coal production fell 42% in 2020, in part due to a 91-day strike at a major northern mine combined with COVID-19 pandemic disruptions; Colombia was nonetheless the fourth-largest coal exporter in the world that year, after Australia, Indonesia, and Russia, and was the largest single source of U.S. coal imports, supplying about 71% of the total, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In June and September 2020, lawyers for the local Wayuu community and several United Nations independent human-rights experts called for a temporary halt to Cerrejón's mining operations, citing environmental damage from coal dust and water pollution and its effects on the health and rights of indigenous residents of La Guajira.

In March 2025, Glencore announced it would cut annual production at Cerrejón by 5-10 million tonnes, to a range of about 11-16 million tonnes, citing unsustainably low seaborne thermal coal prices; Glencore CEO Gary Nagle attributed the cut to weak global coal pricing rather than any operational or logistics disruption, per Reuters and MiningMX reporting.
paths.estimated_global_share: Colombia produced 54 million short tons of coal in 2020, with the great majority exported (75 million short tons of exports that year, drawing down stockpiles), and coal has been the country's second-largest export commodity by value since 2001, after oil and petroleum products. In 2021, Colombia was South America's largest coal producer, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration and Wikipedia's tabulation of BP Statistical Review of World Energy data.
