paths.name: Germany and Poland's Declining Domestic Coal-Fired Power
origin_regions: Germany (Rhineland lignite basin near Cologne, including the Hambach and Garzweiler open-pit mines; Lusatia lignite basin in eastern Germany)
Poland (Upper Silesian Coal Basin; Bełchatów lignite mine and power station)
chokepoints: Germany's legislated coal phase-out, under which the government's Commission on Growth, Structural Change and Employment set a target in January 2019 to shut down the country's remaining coal-fired power plants by 2038
The EU Emissions Trading System carbon price, which raises the marginal cost of coal-fired generation relative to gas and renewables and can force early plant retirements

The EU Methane Regulation, which since 2025 has imposed new measurement and reporting requirements on coal mine methane emissions from German and Polish mines, adding compliance costs that could accelerate closures

Bełchatów, Europe's largest coal-fired power station, whose output depends on a single adjacent lignite strip mine, creating a concentrated single-site dependency for a significant share of Polish electricity
paths.why_it_matters: Germany and Poland are the European Union's two largest coal producers and consumers, and both are winding down coal-fired power generation as wind and solar capacity expands, but from very different starting points and at different speeds. Germany ended domestic hard coal (Steinkohle) mining entirely in 2018 after a government decision to phase out mining subsidies, and now relies on lignite mined in the Rhineland and Lusatia basins plus imports for its remaining coal plants, which are being retired on a path to 2038. Poland still generates roughly half its electricity from coal, more slowly diversifying away from a fuel that underpins both grid reliability and coal-region employment, so its transition carries greater near-term energy-security and social stakes. Because Germany and Poland have historically been among the largest coal consumers in Europe, their declining coal burn is steadily shrinking one of the world's largest thermal coal demand centers, a supply/demand-side shift that reduces the addressable market for coal-exporting countries.
historical_precedents: In February 2007, Germany announced plans to phase out hard coal-mining subsidies by 2018, a decision that ended domestic hard coal mining in the country entirely; in January 2019, Germany's Commission on Growth, Structural Change and Employment recommended phasing out and shutting down the country's remaining 84 coal-fired power plants by 2038, per Wikipedia's sourced account of German government decisions.

In October 2018, a German court halted planned clearance of the ancient Hambach Forest to allow expansion of the adjacent Hambach lignite mine, after large-scale protests; the ruling required further review before any resumption of clearance, per Wikipedia's sourced account of the dispute.
paths.estimated_global_share: Coal's share of Germany's electricity generation fell from 52% in 2000 to 21% in 2025, an all-time low, even as Germany remained the European Union's largest coal-producing country; clean sources supplied 59% of German electricity in 2025, below the EU average of 71%, per the energy think tank Ember. In Poland, coal's share of electricity fell from 91% two decades ago to 51% in 2025, a roughly 30-percentage-point drop over the preceding decade, with fossil fuels overall supplying 69% of Polish electricity in 2025; Poland also contributed 65% of the European Union's total coal mine methane emissions in 2023, one of the highest shares of any country globally, per Ember.

paths.name: Global Methanol Production and Trade Network
origin_regions: Trinidad and Tobago (Point Lisas Industrial Estate)
chokepoints: Trinidad and Tobago natural gas supply contracts (Point Lisas methanol complex dependent on National Gas Company allocations)
China's concentrated coal-to-methanol/methanol-to-olefins (MTO) production base
Strait of Hormuz (for Middle East methanol and feedstock-gas exports)
destination_regions: global chemical derivatives manufacturing (formaldehyde, acetic acid, MTBE, olefins)
paths.why_it_matters: Methanol is one of the world's highest-volume traded chemical commodities, used as a base building block for formaldehyde, acetic acid, and MTBE, as feedstock for China's methanol-to-olefins (MTO) plastics route, and increasingly as a marine and vehicle fuel. China is both the industry's dominant producer (largely coal-based) and its largest importer, so Chinese demand and domestic capacity additions move global prices, while methanol production outside China is unusually concentrated in a handful of natural-gas-advantaged locations, chiefly Trinidad and Tobago and the Middle East, that ship into that Chinese-anchored market. Trinidad in particular has supplied methanol to the U.S. and world markets for decades, but its aging natural-gas fields have gone into steep decline, squeezing feedstock for its methanol plants and illustrating how a single country's upstream gas depletion can idle a major share of the Western Hemisphere's methanol capacity.
historical_precedents: On June 29, 2026, Methanex Corporation announced it would indefinitely idle its 860,000-tonne-per-year Titan methanol plant at Point Lisas, Trinidad and Tobago, after being unable to secure a new natural gas supply agreement with the state-owned National Gas Company before its existing contract's Q3 2026 expiry; the company's Atlas joint-venture plant (63.1% Methanex-owned) was already idled in a preserved state at the time, per Methanex's investor press release (reproduced by StockTitan) and the Trinidad Guardian.

Trinidad and Tobago's dry natural gas production fell by nearly 70% between its 2013 peak of 1.51 trillion cubic feet and 2024, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data cited by ICIS, driving the feedstock shortage behind the Titan and Atlas idlings; new offshore gas fields operated by bp (Ginger, Mento) and Shell (Aphrodite, Manatee) are expected online in 2027 and could allow idled units to restart if conditions improve.
paths.estimated_global_share: Global methanol production capacity in 2023 is estimated at approximately 135 million tonnes per Methanol Institute reporting citing S&P Global data, or nearly 146 million tonnes (excluding coal-to-olefins/coal-to-propylene captive capacity) per Argus Media's Methanol Analytics report -- the roughly 8% gap reflects differing treatment of China's large captive CTO/CTP capacity rather than a genuine data conflict. China accounted for 52% of 2023 global capacity (76 million tonnes) per Argus, with the Middle East second at 18% (26 million tonnes) and Latin America and the Caribbean, including Trinidad and Tobago, third at 8% (12 million tonnes). China's methanol imports reached a historical record of 14 million tonnes in 2023, per the Methanol Institute's 2024 Milestones report.

paths.name: Global Chlor-Alkali (Chlorine and Caustic Soda) Supply Chain
commodities: hydrochloric acid and other chlor-alkali derivatives
origin_regions: United States Gulf Coast and industrial belt (Olin, Westlake, Occidental Chemical/OxyChem plants)
Europe (Euro Chlor member sites across 19 countries)
chokepoints: Small number of large chlor-alkali producers (Olin, Westlake, OxyChem in the U.S.) operating 49 U.S. plants as of 2019
Electricity-intensive electrolysis process, exposing output to power-grid disruptions and storms
Limited economical long-distance transport of liquefied chlorine gas (moved primarily by dedicated rail tank car within North America), meaning production outages cannot easily be offset by imports
destination_regions: domestic manufacturing of PVC, epoxies, and other organic/inorganic chemicals
water treatment and municipal wastewater disinfection
United States, Canada, and Mexico (largest chlorine trade partners to each other)
paths.why_it_matters: The chlor-alkali process, which splits sodium chloride brine by electrolysis into chlorine gas, hydrogen, and caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), underpins a huge share of the chemical industry: chlorine is the essential building block for PVC plastic, and caustic soda is a critical industrial input for everything from pulp and paper to alumina refining and soap manufacturing. Because chlorine is hazardous to store and ship long distances (it is typically moved as a liquefied gas by dedicated rail tank car and has only a 6-12 month shelf life), production is geographically concentrated and effectively must be consumed close to where it is made, so weather or grid disruptions at a handful of U.S. Gulf Coast and European plants can tighten downstream PVC, water-treatment-chemical, and pulp-and-paper supply with little ability for imports to compensate.
historical_precedents: Winter Storm Uri struck the U.S. Gulf Coast in February 2021 and caused a temporary loss of approximately 28% of domestic chlor-alkali production capacity, compounding pandemic-driven demand increases for chlorine-based disinfection products, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Chlorine Supply Chain profile (citing the Chlorine Institute).

In the spring, summer, and later months of 2021, a series of equipment failures at chlor-alkali plants in West Virginia, Utah, and Washington caused further temporary production losses, followed by permanent chlor-alkali capacity reductions at facilities in New York, Alabama, Louisiana, and Texas, per the same EPA profile.
paths.estimated_global_share: U.S. domestic chlorine production totaled approximately 10,000 million kilograms in 2019 across 49 domestic manufacturing locations, with the U.S. ranking first worldwide in chlorine imports (305 million kilograms) and third worldwide in exports (44 million kilograms) in 2021 -- behind Canada, the world's largest chlorine exporter at 275 million kilograms -- per the EPA's Chlorine Supply Chain profile citing Chlorine Institute and World Bank WITS trade data. In Europe, Euro Chlor's roughly 60 member manufacturing sites across 19 countries held about 11 million tonnes of chlorine capacity and produced 8,041 kilotonnes of chlorine in the most recent full year reported. As of 2021, membrane-cell technology accounted for 46% of U.S. chlorine production, asbestos diaphragm-cell technology for 36%, and non-asbestos diaphragm-cell technology for 1%, per the EPA.

paths.name: Global Beef Export Corridor (Brazil / Australia / India)
origin_regions: Brazilian cattle-ranching states (Mato Grosso, Goias, and other Center-West/South regions)

paths.why_it_matters: A handful of exporting countries supply most of the world's traded beef, and an even more concentrated set of buyers -- led by China, the world's largest beef importer -- absorbs it, so the corridor is unusually sensitive to shifts in any single link. USDA forecasts the top five beef exporters (Brazil, Australia, India, Argentina, and New Zealand) will together supply about 69 percent of forecast global beef exports of 13.8 million metric tons in 2026, while China alone is forecast to account for roughly 27 percent of global beef imports; a change in Chinese import policy, a herd-health event, or a cross-border livestock restriction can therefore quickly reprice beef for feedlots, retailers, and consumers worldwide.
historical_precedents: In 2026, China -- the world's largest beef importer -- began implementing tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) that USDA forecasts will cut its beef imports by 13 percent year-over-year, with Brazil and Australia (the two largest global beef exporters) most exposed to the change; despite the new TRQs and a forecast 2 percent decline in Brazilian production from a record 2025, Brazil's and Australia's beef exports were forecast down only 2 percent as both redirected supply toward robust US import demand, according to USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service.

A closure of the US-Mexico border to live cattle imports, still in effect heading into 2026, left more slaughter-ready cattle available inside Mexico; USDA forecasts this will lift Mexican beef production 11 percent and Mexican beef exports 23 percent in 2026, even as the same restriction on cattle inflows to US feedlots contributes to a forecast 1 percent decline in US beef production and 8 percent decline in US beef exports that year.
paths.estimated_global_share: USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service forecasts Brazil will remain the world's largest beef producer (about 12.4 million metric tons, carcass-weight equivalent, in 2026) and largest exporter (4.275 million metric tons, roughly 31 percent of forecast 2026 global beef exports of 13.8 million metric tons), followed by Australia (2.16 million metric tons, about 16 percent) and India (1.7 million metric tons of carabeef, about 12 percent); China is forecast to import about 3.2 million metric tons, roughly 27 percent of forecast 2026 global beef imports of 11.68 million metric tons.

paths.name: Brazil's Near-Monopoly on Niobium for Steel and Aerospace Superalloys
chokepoints: Single-country mine and reserve dominance in Brazil, about 92% of global mine production
Historic concentration of Brazil's output in a single company, CBMM, which operates the Araxá deposit
No substitute for niobium's role in high-strength low-alloy steel microalloying without a performance or cost penalty
destination_regions: global steelmaking and aerospace superalloy manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Niobium, mostly consumed as ferroniobium, is a low-dose but essential input for the high-strength low-alloy steel used in pipelines, automobiles, and construction, and, in metal form, for the nickel-based superalloys used in jet engines. Brazil holds the overwhelming majority of both world mine production and reserves, and for decades that supply has been concentrated in a single company, CBMM, operating the Araxá deposit in Minas Gerais. Because there is no substitute for niobium's steel-strengthening role without added cost or a loss of performance, and because Canada is the only other producer of any scale, a disruption to Brazilian output would leave global steelmakers with few near-term alternatives.
historical_precedents: In 2011, a consortium of Chinese, Japanese, and South Korean steelmaking and trading companies paid an estimated $4 billion for a 30% stake in CBMM, the Brazilian company that supplies the large majority of world niobium, reflecting the strategic value major steel-consuming economies placed on securing long-term access to Brazilian supply.

A 2009 U.S. State Department diplomatic cable on 'critical foreign dependencies,' published via WikiLeaks in 2010, listed Brazil's Araxá and Catalão niobium mines among the foreign mineral facilities the United States considered essential to its national security, illustrating how long supply-chain planners have treated Brazil's niobium dominance as a single-point-of-failure risk.
paths.estimated_global_share: Brazil accounted for an estimated 92% of world niobium mine production in 2024 (100,000 of 110,000 metric tons) and roughly 94% of world reserves (16,000,000 of a rounded >17,000,000 metric tons), per the U.S. Geological Survey; Canada supplied nearly all of the remainder, about 6-7% of production

paths.why_it_matters: Chromium has no substitute in stainless steel, its dominant end use, or in the superalloys used in jet engines and other high-temperature applications. South Africa and Kazakhstan together hold about 95% of world chromium resources and account for the majority of mined chromite, most of which is exported as ore to China for conversion into ferrochromium and stainless steel. South Africa's chromite and ferrochrome sector has been repeatedly strained by Eskom's rolling electricity blackouts, since ferrochrome smelting is highly power-intensive, while China's growing ferrochrome-smelting capacity and stainless-steel oversupply have squeezed South African producers' margins and market share.
historical_precedents: In October 2023, Glencore cut its full-year ferrochrome production guidance by about 8% (from 1.31 million to 1.2 million tons) after South African load-shedding and elevated winter electricity prices forced additional smelter offline days; year-to-date production was already down 21% versus the prior year, per MiningMX.

In 2025, amid Chinese ferrochrome oversupply and South Africa's loss of its long-held position as the world's largest ferrochrome producer to China, South Africa's government moved to pair a proposed chrome-ore export levy with discounted Eskom electricity tariffs for domestic smelters, an attempt to keep more chrome processing (and jobs) onshore rather than exporting raw ore, per Africa Tax Review and Business Insider Africa.

paths.why_it_matters: Indium is refined almost entirely as a byproduct of zinc smelting, and China accounts for the large majority of world refinery output. Its longest-standing use is as indium tin oxide (ITO), the conductive coating on most LCD and touchscreen displays, but a newer and fast-growing use is indium phosphide (InP), the substrate material for the high-speed photonic components that connect AI data-center GPUs. Because China dominates both indium refining and, through companies like AXT, much of world InP substrate manufacturing, its 2025 move to require export licenses for InP has become a real bottleneck for AI infrastructure buildouts even though indium metal itself remains outside formal export controls.
historical_precedents: In September 2024, the U.S. Trade Representative finalized Section 301 tariff modifications imposing a 25% tariff on certain Chinese critical minerals, including indium; the share of U.S. indium imports sourced from China rose to 25% that month, up from an average of 8% over the prior four years, while the average U.S. warehouse indium price rose 42% over the year to $340 per kilogram, peaking at $420 per kilogram in June 2024, per the U.S. Geological Survey.

China placed indium phosphide under export-licensing controls in February 2025. By May 2026, AXT, the world's second-largest InP substrate producer, said InP export permits had become 'the most significant challenge we currently face,' noting its Chinese subsidiary received its first export permits only in June 2025 and still faced a significant order backlog, disrupting supply to photonics makers serving the AI data-center buildout, per Reuters reporting.

paths.name: Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen-Class) Single-Source Manufacturing Concentration
commodities: epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPen and authorized generic devices)
origin_regions: United States (Meridian Medical Technologies, a Pfizer subsidiary - St. Louis, Missouri manufacturing plant)
chokepoints: Mylan (the EpiPen brand owner, now part of Viatris) relied on a single contract manufacturer, Pfizer subsidiary Meridian Medical Technologies, to produce every EpiPen device sold in the U.S. and Canadian markets

Epinephrine auto-injectors are complex pre-filled mechanical delivery devices rather than a simple chemical formulation, so FDA requalification of an alternate manufacturing site cannot happen quickly once a shortage begins
A single facility's corrective-action period following an FDA warning letter directly reduced national device output, with no comparably scaled substitute manufacturer able to absorb the shortfall
paths.why_it_matters: Mylan, the brand owner of the EpiPen, does not manufacture the device itself: every EpiPen sold in the United States and Canada was produced at a single Pfizer subsidiary plant, Meridian Medical Technologies in Missouri, according to Supply Chain Dive's review of the 2017-2019 shortage. Because epinephrine auto-injectors are mechanical delivery devices rather than an easily substituted chemical formulation, a manufacturing quality-control failure at that one facility could not be quickly offset by another supplier, illustrating how concentrating a life-saving, no-substitute emergency-use device in a single production site creates an outsized single point of failure for patients experiencing severe allergic reactions.
historical_precedents: In September 2017, the FDA sent a warning letter to Meridian Medical Technologies stating that the company's 'own data show that [it] received hundreds of complaints that [its] EpiPen products failed to operate during life-threatening emergencies, including some situations in which patients subsequently died,' and citing broader manufacturing quality-control failures at its Missouri plant, per Supply Chain Dive's review of the letter.

Manufacturing delays at Meridian tied to those quality problems produced intermittent EpiPen supply constraints that first caused shortages in Canada in early 2018; the FDA officially added EpiPen to its drug shortage list on 9 May 2018, and Mylan reported its North American sales fell 19% to $985.3 million in the first quarter of 2018, a decline it attributed in part to lower EpiPen sales, per Supply Chain Dive.
paths.estimated_global_share: During the 2017-2019 shortage, a single Pfizer-owned Meridian Medical Technologies plant in Missouri was the sole manufacturing source for Mylan's EpiPen supply to both the U.S. and Canadian markets; contemporaneous reporting identified no comparably scaled alternate manufacturer able to absorb the shortfall, and the disruption affected both countries at the same time, per Supply Chain Dive.

paths.name: Global Vaccine Cold-Chain Equipment Infrastructure Gap
commodities: cold-chain equipment (refrigerators, freezers, cold boxes, vaccine carriers)
origin_regions: Global vaccine manufacturing sites (India, Europe, United States, and other producers)
chokepoints: Health facilities in many lower-income countries lack functioning cold-chain equipment altogether, or operate equipment that does not meet WHO Performance, Quality and Safety (PQS) standards

Vaccine potency is irreversibly lost once temperature excursions occur, so any break in the 2-8°C cold chain between manufacturer and patient can render doses unusable regardless of how much vaccine was produced or shipped
Chronic underinvestment in cold-chain equipment maintenance and replacement, beyond initial equipment deployment, across many national immunization programs
destination_regions: other Gavi-eligible low- and middle-income countries
paths.why_it_matters: Because vaccines lose potency irreversibly once exposed to temperatures outside their required 2-8°C range, delivering life-saving immunizations depends as much on an unbroken chain of refrigeration equipment reaching the last mile as it does on vaccine manufacturing itself. In Kenya, an estimated 18% of health facilities had no cold-chain equipment at all, and 81% of the equipment in use failed to meet WHO Performance, Quality and Safety standards, according to a peer-reviewed evaluation published in Global Health: Science and Practice; in Guinea, only 24% of children aged 12-23 months were fully immunized in 2018, ranging from 8% to 36% by region, reflecting similar last-mile equipment and access gaps. Because this infrastructure gap exists across dozens of lower-income countries simultaneously, it functions as a standing, structural constraint on global immunization coverage independent of any single manufacturer's output.
historical_precedents: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, committed more than US$250 million between 2016 and 2021 through its Cold Chain Equipment Optimisation Platform (CCEOP) to install cold-chain equipment across more than 63,000 health facilities in Gavi-supported countries, according to a peer-reviewed evaluation published in Global Health: Science and Practice; Guinea alone received a $10.9 million CCEOP grant that delivered 848 pieces of cold-chain equipment, and Kenya received an $8.2 million grant that deployed 1,004 refrigerators and freezers to 690 facilities.

Gavi's own independent multi-year evaluation of CCEOP, covering Guinea, Kenya, and Pakistan between a 2018 baseline and a 2021 endline, found the platform succeeded in increasing the number of health facilities with WHO-standard cold-chain equipment and in improving immunization service reliability and vaccine potency, but also concluded that cold-chain equipment maintenance systems required further investment beyond initial deployment to sustain those gains, per Gavi's published evaluation summary.
paths.estimated_global_share: An estimated 18% of health facilities surveyed in Kenya had no cold-chain equipment at all, and 81% of facilities with equipment did not meet WHO Performance, Quality and Safety standards, per a peer-reviewed evaluation in Global Health: Science and Practice; Gavi's Cold Chain Equipment Optimisation Platform invested more than $250 million between 2016 and 2021 to address such gaps across more than 63,000 health facilities in Gavi-supported countries.

origin_regions: United States and Europe (concentrated among a small number of specialized suppliers, including Cytiva, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Sartorius, Pall Corporation, and MilliporeSigma/Merck KGaA)
chokepoints: Global biologics and vaccine manufacturing capacity is concentrated among a small number of specialized single-use plastics and bioprocessing-equipment suppliers, with few qualified alternate sources for custom bioreactor bags and assemblies
COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers' surging demand for single-use bioprocessing components in 2020-2021 competed directly with existing biologics manufacturers for the same limited supplier capacity
Single-use bioprocessing assemblies require lengthy validation and qualification before a biologics manufacturer can switch suppliers, slowing the industry's ability to respond to a shortage
destination_regions: Global biologics and vaccine manufacturers, including COVID-19 vaccine producers
paths.why_it_matters: Modern biologics and vaccine manufacturing relies heavily on single-use plastic bioreactor bags, tubing, and filter assemblies rather than reusable stainless-steel equipment, because disposable systems reduce cross-contamination risk and are faster to bring online - but that same reliance concentrated global biologics production capacity behind a small number of specialized suppliers. When COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers' demand for these components surged in 2020-2021, lead times for single-use bioprocessing equipment stretched to 10 to 12 months industry-wide, according to Bioprocess International, constraining the manufacturing capacity of vaccine producers and other biologics makers competing for the same limited supplier output at the same time.
historical_precedents: By May 2021, lead times for single-use bioprocessing components from major suppliers had stretched to 10, 11, and even 12 months, according to Bioprocess International; even ABEC, a bioreactor-system maker, quoted roughly 16 weeks for custom bioreactor bags amid what it described as a 'significant increase' in demand, particularly for large 4,000-liter mammalian-cell bags used in biologics manufacturing.

In response, major single-use suppliers announced large capacity expansions during 2021: Pall Corporation invested $114 million to increase single-use output capacity, Cytiva announced a $500 million plan to expand biomanufacturing capacity, and MilliporeSigma (Merck KGaA's life-science division) expedited a $30 million expansion in France; Bioprocess International noted these expansions would still take months to come online, meaning shortages were expected to persist through 2021.
paths.estimated_global_share: Global single-use bioprocessing component supply during the 2020-2021 shortage was concentrated among a small number of specialized manufacturers - Cytiva, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Sartorius, Pall Corporation, and MilliporeSigma/Merck KGaA - whose combined lead times stretched to 10-12 months industry-wide at the shortage's peak, according to Bioprocess International; no comparably scaled alternate supplier base existed to absorb the surge in demand from COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers.

paths.name: Egypt Nitrogen Fertilizer Export Corridor (Abu Qir Bay / Mediterranean)
commodities: nitrogenous fertilizers (urea ammonium nitrate, ammonium nitrate)
origin_regions: Abu Qir Bay industrial complex, Alexandria Governorate, Egypt (natural-gas-fed ammonia, urea, and ammonium nitrate plants)
Other nitrogen fertilizer plants along Egypt's Mediterranean coast and Nile Delta
chokepoints: Alexandria-area port and fertilizer export terminals, Egypt
Mediterranean Sea shipping lanes to Europe
Suez Canal (for onward shipments toward Asia and the Red Sea)
destination_regions: Southern and Western Europe (Turkey, Spain, Italy, France, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, United Kingdom, Belgium)
paths.why_it_matters: Egypt has built one of the world's larger ammonia industries by drawing on domestic natural gas to feed a cluster of nitrogen fertilizer plants concentrated on its Mediterranean coast, led by Abu Qir Fertilizers and Chemical Industries Company, which alone accounts for about half of the country's nitrogen fertilizer output from a single industrial complex at Abu Qir Bay near Alexandria. Because Egypt's own agricultural sector cannot absorb this scale of production, several million tonnes of nitrogenous fertilizer are exported each year, worth $1.2 billion to $2.8 billion annually depending on world price cycles, overwhelmingly to Mediterranean and European buyers reached via Alexandria-area ports and Mediterranean shipping lanes. This concentrates a meaningful share of Southern Europe's nitrogen fertilizer supply in a small number of gas-fed plants along one stretch of Egyptian coastline, so a disruption to Egyptian gas supply, port operations, or Mediterranean shipping would be felt quickly by European farmers who have come to rely on Egyptian urea and ammonium nitrate; nitrogen fertilizer has no agricultural substitute.
historical_precedents: 2020-2024: Egypt's exports of nitrogenous fertilizers (Harmonized System code 3102) ranged between about 3.4 million and 4.2 million tonnes a year, and their value swung from $1.16 billion in 2020 to a peak of $2.76 billion in 2022 amid the global natural-gas-linked fertilizer price spike, before easing to $1.55 billion in 2024, per UN Comtrade trade statistics.

2023-2024: Abu Qir Fertilizers and Chemical Industries Company, which produces about 50% of Egypt's nitrogen fertilizer output, was partially privatized in 2023 when Abu Dhabi Developmental Holding Company (21.5%) and Saudi Egyptian Investment Company (19.8%) acquired stakes from the Egyptian state; further stock sales in 2024 reduced the Egyptian government's remaining holding from a controlling stake to a minority position, per Forbes Middle East and Daily News Egypt (via Wikipedia).
paths.estimated_global_share: Egypt produced an estimated 4.0 million of the world's 160 million metric tons of ammonia (nitrogen content) in 2025, about 2.5% of global output and a similar order of magnitude to Saudi Arabia's 5.2 million tons, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (which revised Egypt's 2024 estimate down to 3.9 million tons). In 2024, Egypt's top nitrogenous-fertilizer export markets by value were Turkey ($266 million), Spain ($187 million), Italy ($171 million), France ($166 million), and Romania ($112 million), per UN Comtrade.

paths.name: India Fertilizer Import Dependence and Subsidy System
origin_regions: Gulf states (Oman, United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain) for urea and other nitrogenous fertilizer
Saudi Arabia, Morocco, China, Jordan, and Russia for diammonium phosphate (DAP)
chokepoints: India's government-administered Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme and statutory urea price control, which govern how much imported fertilizer state trading agencies can afford to buy and distribute
Government budget allocation and disbursement timelines for fertilizer subsidy payments
Major fertilizer-handling ports on India's west and east coasts
destination_regions: India (nationwide, concentrated in the wheat- and rice-growing states of North India and the cotton- and rice-growing states elsewhere)
paths.why_it_matters: India is one of the world's largest importers of both urea and diammonium phosphate (DAP), a dependence that persists even though India itself ranks among the top few global ammonia producers, because domestic urea and phosphate-fertilizer capacity has not kept pace with subsidized farm demand. Nearly all of that demand flows through a government subsidy and price-control system that fixes what farmers pay regardless of world prices, so when world fertilizer prices spike, as they did in 2022, the burden falls on India's fertilizer subsidy budget rather than on farmers, and any resulting funding shortfall or disbursement delay can constrain how much state trading agencies are able to import and distribute. Because India's purchases are large enough to move world prices, and its DAP imports alone draw on Saudi Arabia, Morocco, China, Jordan, and Russia -- exporters covered by several other entries in this dataset -- India functions as a demand-side nexus for a large share of the world's traded phosphate and nitrogen fertilizer, distinct from any single exporting country's supply-side restrictions. India's own phosphate rock production, at an estimated 1.5 million of the world's 250 million metric tons in 2025 (about 0.6%), covers only a small fraction of its raw-material needs, reinforcing the country's reliance on imported DAP.
historical_precedents: 2020-2022: India's cif import value of nitrogenous fertilizers (HS 3102) rose from $3.05 billion in 2020 to $7.49 billion in 2022 on import volumes of about 10.9 million tonnes, while DAP (HS 310530) import costs rose from $2.12 billion to $5.97 billion over the same period, tracking the global natural-gas and phosphate price spike; import values eased to $2.47 billion (nitrogenous) and $2.76 billion (DAP) by 2024, per UN Comtrade trade statistics.

2018-2019: A Parliamentary Standing Committee review found that inadequate budget allocation had left Rs 30,244 crore in fertilizer subsidy bills to manufacturers unpaid as of 2018-19, up from Rs 19,363 crore the year before, and recommended shifting toward paying the subsidy directly into farmers' bank accounts rather than to fertilizer companies, per PRS India's summary of the committee's findings.
paths.estimated_global_share: India's 2024 fertilizer import bill included $2.47 billion of nitrogenous fertilizers (HS 3102), sourced mainly from Oman ($898 million), Russia ($537 million), the United Arab Emirates ($208 million), Qatar ($193 million), and Saudi Arabia ($190 million), and $2.76 billion of diammonium phosphate (HS 310530), sourced mainly from Saudi Arabia (about 40% of import value), Morocco (about 28%), and China (about 19%), per UN Comtrade trade statistics.

paths.name: Turkey Boron/Borate Export Corridor (Micronutrient Fertilizer Feedstock)
origin_regions: Boron mining and processing districts of western Turkey, including Bigadic, mined and refined exclusively by state-owned Eti Maden
chokepoints: Eti Maden's state-granted legal monopoly on all boron mining and processing within Turkey
Eti Maden's Ab Etiproducts Oy export subsidiary and its Baltic and Black Sea warehouse/terminal network
destination_regions: Global fertilizer, glass, ceramics, and detergent manufacturing centers, including the United States, China, Europe (Scandinavia, Baltic states), Africa, and former Soviet states
paths.why_it_matters: Boron has no substitute as a micronutrient fertilizer for boron-responsive crops such as cotton, fruit, and vegetables, and it is also essential to glass, ceramics, and detergent manufacturing -- uses that together with fertilizer account for more than three-quarters of world boron consumption. Turkey holds the large majority of the world's economically viable boron reserves and remains by far the largest single national source of refined borate, all of it mined and processed under the exclusive legal monopoly of one state-owned company, Eti Maden. Because there is no comparable alternative source at meaningful scale and the entire supply chain runs through a single company's mines, processing plants, and export network, Turkish government policy or an operational disruption at Eti Maden would directly affect the availability of boron micronutrient fertilizer, along with glass and detergent feedstock, for buyers worldwide.
historical_precedents: 2023-2024: Turkey opened two new boron processing facilities within about 18 months -- a boron carbide plant in March 2023 and the Bigadic Granular Boron Production Facility in September 2024, the latter built with 35,000 tons/year of capacity to produce granulated boron products specifically for the fertilizer industry (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025).

2024-2025: USGS's estimate of Turkey's refined borate production was revised down to 1.8 million metric tons for 2024 (from an initial 3.0-million-ton estimate published a year earlier) and fell further to an estimated 1.5 million tons in 2025, even as Turkey's reported boron reserves of 950 million metric tons -- still by far the world's largest -- were left unrevised, illustrating the volatility that can affect output from the world's dominant, single-country boron supply base (USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

As of 2012, Eti Maden's share of global borate mineral production was estimated at 47%, more than double the 23% share of its nearest competitor, Rio Tinto Group, reflecting the concentration of world boron supply under Turkey's state mining monopoly (Wikipedia, citing company and industry data).
paths.estimated_global_share: Turkey held an estimated 950 million of the roughly 1.09 billion metric tons of boron reserves reported by USGS across producing countries in 2025 -- about 87% of reported reserves, and roughly seven times the next-largest reserve base (Russia, at 40 million tons). Turkey's 2025 production of 1.5 million metric tons of refined borates accounted for about half of the combined output reported by all USGS-listed producer countries (a total of about 2.9 million tons, since the United States withholds its production data), still more than any other single country. Turkey supplied about 90% of all U.S. boron imports from 2021 to 2024, per USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026.

paths.name: Japan-Germany-China Industrial Robotics Manufacturing Route
origin_regions: Japan (Fanuc, Yaskawa Electric, Kawasaki Heavy Industries, and Mitsubishi Electric manufacturing base)
China (Jiangsu, Guangdong, and Liaoning province clusters - fast-growing domestic suppliers plus KUKA's own Foshan plant)
chokepoints: Japan's roughly 38% share of world industrial-robot production, concentrated in a handful of manufacturers
KUKA, Germany's flagship robot maker, has been majority-owned by China's Midea Group since 2016-2017, blurring the line between the German and Chinese ends of this supply chain
China's rapid buildout of domestic robot-manufacturing capacity, which for the first time in 2024 outsold foreign suppliers inside China's own market
destination_regions: global automotive and electronics assembly plants
paths.why_it_matters: Industrial robots -- the articulated arms that weld car bodies, place electronic components, and handle materials on assembly lines worldwide -- are manufactured by a small set of companies concentrated in Japan (Fanuc, Yaskawa, Kawasaki, Mitsubishi Electric), historically also Germany (KUKA), and an increasingly self-sufficient China. This differs from the machine-tool and semiconductor-equipment routes already in this dataset: it is about the capital equipment that automates factories themselves, so a disruption to robot supply constrains how quickly manufacturers anywhere can add or replace automation capacity. The 2016-2017 acquisition of KUKA by China's Midea Group already shifted one of the industry's historic centers of gravity toward China, and China's domestic robot makers have since scaled up quickly enough to begin displacing Japanese and European suppliers inside China itself, the world's largest robot market.
historical_precedents: Midea Group of China acquired Germany's KUKA, one of the world's best-known industrial robot makers, beginning with a 2016 tender offer and completing a controlling stake in early 2017; the deal prompted Germany to tighten its foreign-investment screening rules for critical technologies and later, KUKA shifted new production capacity toward a China-based plant in Foshan.

For the first time on record, Chinese-made robots outsold foreign-made robots inside China's own market in 2024: domestic manufacturers' share of China's industrial-robot installations climbed to 57%, up from 47% in 2023, per the IFR's World Robotics 2025 report.
paths.estimated_global_share: Japan accounts for roughly 38% of global industrial-robot production, per the International Federation of Robotics' World Robotics 2024 report; China installed 295,000 industrial robots in 2024 alone (up 7% year-on-year), representing 54% of global robot demand and pushing China's total operational robot stock to a world-record 2,027,000 units, per the IFR's World Robotics 2025 report.

paths.name: China's Dominance of Refined Tellurium for Solar and Thermoelectric Uses
origin_regions: Sweden, Russia, Japan, and Uzbekistan (smaller-volume byproduct recovery)
chokepoints: China's dominance of world refined tellurium output, an estimated three-quarters of global production in 2024
Tellurium is recovered almost entirely as a minor byproduct of electrolytic copper refining, so its supply cannot expand independently of copper-refining capacity
destination_regions: global cadmium telluride (CdTe) thin-film solar-panel manufacturing, including domestic U.S. production
global thermoelectric device and specialty-metallurgical manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Tellurium is a minor-volume metal recovered almost entirely as a byproduct of electrolytic copper refining, making its output structurally tied to copper-smelting decisions rather than dedicated tellurium mining. It is the essential semiconductor material in cadmium telluride (CdTe), a leading thin-film solar-panel technology, and in bismuth telluride thermoelectric coolers. China refines the large majority of the world's tellurium alongside its expanding copper-smelting industry, giving it substantial influence over pricing and availability for a material with no ready substitute in CdTe solar cells, even though tellurium volumes are too small to attract the export-control attention given to other Chinese-dominated critical minerals.
historical_precedents: More than 90% of tellurium is recovered from anode slimes generated during electrolytic copper refining; China's refined tellurium output has grown substantially over the past decade alongside a roughly 60% increase in its electrolytically refined copper production capacity and a near-doubling of its copper anode capacity, per the U.S. Geological Survey.

In 2024, limited tellurium availability outside North America and the higher cost of purchasing tellurium from China pushed the average European tellurium price up about 4% to an estimated $80 per kilogram, even as the well-supplied North American market saw prices ease 5% to about $75 per kilogram, per the U.S. Geological Survey.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for an estimated 75% of world refined tellurium output in 2024 (750 of a 980-metric-ton world total, which the USGS notes excludes several producing countries with inadequate data), per the U.S. Geological Survey; solar power cells accounted for an estimated 60% of global tellurium consumption in 2024, primarily as cadmium telluride (CdTe) thin-film photovoltaic material, with thermoelectric devices accounting for another 20%.

sources.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025: Tellurium

paths.name: China's Dominance of Primary Aluminum Smelting
origin_regions: Russia, India, Canada, United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain (smaller-volume primary smelting)
chokepoints: China's dominance of world primary aluminum smelter production and yearend capacity, roughly 60% and 57% of the global totals respectively
Aluminum smelting is highly electricity-intensive, so smelter output is directly exposed to national energy-supply and energy-policy decisions in producing countries
2024 U.S. and allied trade actions restricting Russian- and Chinese-origin aluminum from Western markets and metal exchanges
destination_regions: global transportation, packaging, construction, and electrical-equipment manufacturing
paths.why_it_matters: Primary aluminum smelting is one of the most electricity-intensive heavy industries in the world, and China now accounts for roughly six in ten tons of primary aluminum smelted globally. Aluminum underpins transportation, packaging, construction, and electrical applications, and while the raw bauxite ore that feeds alumina refining is geographically dispersed across several countries, the energy-intensive smelting step that turns alumina into metal has consolidated heavily in China, giving it substantial influence over global aluminum supply and pricing even though the United States and its allies source most of their own imported metal from Canada rather than China directly.
historical_precedents: In April 2024, the United States coordinated with the United Kingdom to ban imports of Russian-origin aluminum into both countries and to restrict the sale of Russian aluminum on global metal exchanges and in over-the-counter derivatives trading, per the U.S. Geological Survey.

In July 2024, the United States imposed a 10% duty on aluminum products imported from Mexico where the primary or secondary country of smelt, or the most recent country of cast, was Belarus, China, Iran, or Russia; in September 2024, the United States separately raised tariffs on aluminum products imported directly from China from a range of 0%-7.5% to 25%, per the U.S. Geological Survey.
paths.estimated_global_share: China accounted for an estimated 43.0 million of the world's 72.0 million metric tons of primary aluminum smelter production in 2024 (about 60%) and 44.7 million of 78.4 million metric tons of yearend smelter capacity (about 57%), per the U.S. Geological Survey; U.S. primary production was only 670,000 metric tons in 2024, and the United States was 47% net import-reliant for aluminum, sourcing 56% of its 2020-2023 imports from Canada versus about 3% from China.

paths.name: Oncology Generic Sterile Injectable Chemotherapy Drug Shortages
commodities: generic sterile injectable chemotherapy drugs (e.g. cisplatin, carboplatin, methotrexate, leucovorin, dacarbazine, fludarabine phosphate, azacitidine)
other low-margin generic oncology supportive-care injectables
origin_regions: India (Intas Pharmaceuticals/Accord Healthcare, Cipla, Dr. Reddy's, and other generic sterile-injectable manufacturing plants)
United States (Teva, Pfizer, Fresenius Kabi, and other domestic sterile-injectable manufacturing plants)
small number of additional overseas manufacturing sites (including China and Israel)
chokepoints: Persistent thin profit margins on generic sterile injectable oncology drugs discourage manufacturers from maintaining backup capacity or staying in the market - a 2025 peer-reviewed analysis in Cancer Journal found essential injectable cancer drugs in shortage cost an average of about $2 per vial, versus roughly $1,423 for comparable non-shortage cancer drugs

Extreme few-manufacturer concentration for individual drugs - the same 2025 Cancer Journal study found all identified U.S. manufacturers of cisplatin (6 of 6) and of azacitidine (9 of 9) were reporting shortages simultaneously, and that more than 80% of the oncology drugs it studied had experienced at least one manufacturer exit the market before the shortage began

Manufacturing-quality failures at concentrated overseas plants, most notably an FDA inspection of Intas Pharmaceuticals' India facility supplying Accord Pharma (roughly a third of the U.S. injectable methotrexate market before 2022), which found quality-control records that were "discarded, missing, and purposefully destroyed," according to a 2025 multinational survey published in The Oncologist

Hospital pharmaceutical purchasing is itself concentrated - the 2025 Cancer Journal analysis found Group Purchasing Organizations control an estimated 90% of U.S. hospital pharmaceutical procurement through just four major organizations, reinforcing low-price, single-supplier contracting that leaves little room for redundant capacity
Complex, hazardous, and capital-intensive sterile cytotoxic manufacturing processes that limit the number of facilities able or willing to produce these drugs at all
destination_regions: United States (hospital and community oncology practices)
other high- and middle-income countries with comparable dependence on the same concentrated generic sterile-injectable manufacturing base
paths.why_it_matters: Generic sterile injectable chemotherapy and supportive-care drugs - decades-old, off-patent medicines such as cisplatin, carboplatin, and methotrexate that remain first-line therapy for many cancers - are produced by only a handful of manufacturers worldwide because their low price offers little commercial incentive to enter or remain in the market. The FDA reported 98 active and ongoing U.S. drug shortages at the end of 2024, according to a 2025 peer-reviewed policy analysis in Cancer Journal, and a companion 2025 study in JCO Oncology Practice found that 54% of surveyed National Cancer Institute Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP) practices (49 of 93) had been seriously affected by a drug shortage in the prior three months, most often involving carboplatin (24.7% of practices), leucovorin (22.6%), and cisplatin (19.4%). Because these drugs have no clinically equivalent substitute for many regimens, the same Cancer Journal analysis found roughly three-quarters of oncology pharmacists report that shortages force dose reductions, treatment delays, or regimen changes - and a separate 2025 study found seven of twenty WHO Essential Medicines List cancer drugs are three to five times more likely to face a shortage than the average medicine.
historical_precedents: In mid-2022, an FDA inspection of Intas Pharmaceuticals' sterile-injectable plant in India, which supplied Accord Pharma's roughly one-third share of the U.S. injectable methotrexate market, found manufacturing-quality-control records that had been "discarded, missing, and purposefully destroyed," according to a 2025 multinational survey of Children's Oncology Group institutions published in The Oncologist; the company's subsequent voluntary production halt eliminated a large share of U.S. methotrexate supply and coincided with parallel cisplatin and carboplatin shortages, and the COG survey found 76% of 67 responding U.S. pediatric oncology institutions were affected, with some unable to accept new patient referrals.

Teva's 2021 closure of its Irvine, California sterile-manufacturing plant over mold and sterilization lapses eliminated more than 15% of the U.S. supply of streptozocin and contributed to a dacarbazine shortage in a market that relies on just three producers, according to the 2025 Cancer Journal analysis of oncology drug-shortage drivers - illustrating how a single facility's quality failure can propagate across multiple, seemingly unrelated cancer drugs made at the same plant.
paths.estimated_global_share: A 2025 peer-reviewed Cancer Journal analysis found all identified U.S. manufacturers of cisplatin (6 of 6) and azacitidine (9 of 9) were reporting shortages simultaneously, and that more than 80% of the oncology drugs it studied had at least one manufacturer exit the market before the shortage began; separately, Accord Pharma - supplied by a single Intas Pharmaceuticals plant in India - held roughly one-third of the U.S. injectable methotrexate market before a 2022 quality-driven shutdown, per a 2025 multinational survey published in The Oncologist.

paths.name: Philippines' Coal-Fired Power Generation and Thermal Coal Imports
chokepoints: Near-single-country sourcing of imports: Indonesia supplied 99.46% of the Philippines' coal imports in 2024
Semirara Mining and Power Corporation's effective monopoly on domestic coal production, concentrated on Semirara Island
Seaborne shipping routes from Kalimantan's export ports across the Sulu and South China Seas to Philippine coal-fired plants
Coal-fired plants' large and growing share of installed power-generating capacity, raising the stakes of any import disruption for grid reliability
destination_regions: Philippines (national power grid, spanning the Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao systems)
paths.why_it_matters: Coal supplied 62.5% of the Philippines' electricity generation in 2024, more than every other fuel source combined, and coal-fired capacity keeps expanding even after a 2020 government moratorium on new coal-plant permits. Because domestic mines, chiefly Semirara Mining and Power Corporation's operations on Semirara Island, cannot keep pace with demand, the Philippines imports roughly 95% of the coal it actually burns, and in 2024 essentially all of that (99.46%) came from a single country, Indonesia. That concentration leaves the fuel behind most of the country's baseload power supply dependent on one foreign supplier's mines, ports, and export policy, a vulnerability the Philippine government itself has moved to manage: in July 2026 Manila's energy secretary traveled to Jakarta to seek assurances that new Indonesian coal-export regulations, due to take effect in the first quarter of 2027, would not disrupt existing long-term supply contracts.
historical_precedents: The Philippines imported 39.87 million metric tons of coal in 2024, up from 35.53 MMT in 2023, 32.91 MMT in 2022, 31.43 MMT in 2021, and 28.86 MMT in 2020, a near-uninterrupted rise that has made the country steadily more reliant on seaborne supply even as domestic output plateaued, per the Philippine Department of Energy as reported by the Philippine Daily Inquirer.

In July 2026, the Philippine Department of Energy sent officials led by Energy Secretary Sharon Garin to Jakarta after Indonesia signaled new coal-export guidelines set to take effect in the first quarter of 2027; the Philippines, which sources about 99% of its imported coal from Indonesia, sought and received assurances that existing long-term supply contracts would be honored, per the Philippine Star and the Philippine Daily Inquirer.
paths.estimated_global_share: Coal accounted for 62.5% of Philippine electricity generation in 2024 (79,359 of 126,941 gigawatt-hours) and about 44% of installed generating capacity (13,006 of 29,706 megawatts). The country imported roughly 40.4 million tonnes of coal that year, of which Indonesia supplied about 40.1 million tonnes (99.46%), up from a 98.00% share in 2023; the Philippines' overall energy self-sufficiency ratio fell to 39% in 2024 from 42% in 2023, per the Philippine Department of Energy's 2024 Key Energy Statistics.

paths.name: Peru Anchoveta Fishmeal and Fish Oil Export Corridor
origin_regions: Peru's north-central Pacific coast (Humboldt Current anchoveta fishing grounds)
chokepoints: Peru's government-set anchoveta fishing-season quotas, regulated by IMARPE (the Peruvian Sea Institute) and PRODUCE (the Production Ministry)
Pacific coast fishmeal and fish oil reduction (processing) plants that convert the catch before export
destination_regions: other Asian and global aquaculture and livestock feed markets
paths.why_it_matters: Peru's anchoveta fishery is the world's largest single source of fishmeal and fish oil, key protein and lipid inputs for farmed shrimp and fish feed and livestock feed worldwide, and FAO's GLOBEFISH program identifies Peruvian anchoveta as the primary global source of both commodities. Because the fishery is concentrated in one country's coastal waters and highly sensitive to El Nino-driven ocean warming, a poor anchoveta season can sharply tighten global fishmeal and fish oil supply and raise feed costs for aquaculture producers worldwide, with China — by far the largest buyer of Peruvian fishmeal — especially exposed.
historical_precedents: Global fishmeal production fell 23 percent and fish oil output fell 21 percent in 2023, largely due to poor catches of Peruvian anchoveta following El Nino-driven ocean warming that disrupted Peru's fishing season, according to FAO's GLOBEFISH market analysis.

Supplies recovered as catches improved: Peruvian fishmeal exports rose to 421,000 tonnes in the first quarter of 2025, a 67 percent increase year-on-year, with China receiving 67 percent of Peru's fishmeal exports and 27 percent of its fish oil exports, while Peru's second 2025 fishing-season quota for its North-Centre region was set at 1.63 million metric tons in November 2025, according to FAO GLOBEFISH and the International Fishmeal and Fish Oil Organisation (IFFO). By the first half of 2026, FAO GLOBEFISH reported that reduced quotas in Peru and Chile and rising El Nino risk had tightened global fishmeal and fish oil markets more than at any point since the 2023 disruption.
paths.estimated_global_share: Peru typically supplies around 20 percent of global fishmeal production in an average year, against projected 2025 global output of about 5.6 million tons of fishmeal and 1.2-1.3 million tons of fish oil, according to the International Fishmeal and Fish Oil Organisation (IFFO).

paths.name: Global Tea Export Corridor (Kenya / Sri Lanka / India)
origin_regions: Sri Lanka's central highlands tea estates
Assam and Darjeeling tea-growing regions, India
chokepoints: Mombasa Tea Auction, Kenya
Colombo Tea Auction, Sri Lanka
paths.why_it_matters: Tea is a major export earner and smallholder livelihood source for Kenya, Sri Lanka, and India, together among the world's largest black tea exporters, and small-scale farmers produce roughly 60 percent of the world's tea, according to FAO. Much of this trade is funneled through a small number of auction houses, led by the Mombasa Tea Auction — described by industry reporting as the principal marketplace for tea produced across East and Central Africa — and the Colombo Tea Auction, through which about 90 percent of Sri Lanka's tea crop is exported. Because black tea exports are this concentrated, a weather shock, input-cost shock, or economic disruption in any one of the three countries can move world tea supply and prices and squeeze the incomes of millions of smallholder farmers.
historical_precedents: Sri Lanka, then the world's second-largest black tea exporter, saw its tea production fall 15.6 percent in 2022 — the sharpest crop shortfall since 1995 — after the government's 2021 fertilizer import ban curtailed yields, compounding an economic crisis that further disrupted the country's tea industry; Sri Lankan tea shipments fell 12.5 percent in 2022 to their lowest level since 1996, according to the FAO Intergovernmental Group on Tea's 25th session report (2024).

The resulting supply disruption contributed to the FAO Composite Tea Price rising 14.5 percent in 2022 to USD 2.80 per kilogram, before prices eased 9.2 percent in 2023 as global availability recovered, according to the same FAO report.
paths.estimated_global_share: China and India account for nearly 50 percent and about 20.5 percent of world tea production respectively, while Kenya and Sri Lanka were the world's two largest black tea exporters in 2022, shipping 542,561 and 255,973 tonnes respectively out of 1.84 million tonnes in total world tea exports that year, according to the FAO Intergovernmental Group on Tea's 25th session report (2024). Roughly 90 percent of Sri Lanka's tea crop and 95 percent of its marketed production are sold through the Colombo Tea Auction, according to the Colombo Tea Traders Association.

paths.name: Kirkuk-Ceyhan (Iraq-Turkey) Pipeline
origin_regions: Iraq (Kurdistan Region and Kirkuk fields, northern Iraq)
chokepoints: Iraq-Turkey Pipeline (ITP / Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline)
destination_regions: onward seaborne export to global markets
paths.why_it_matters: The Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline (also called the Iraq-Turkey Pipeline, or ITP) is the principal overland export route for crude oil produced in Iraq's Kurdistan Region and the northern Kirkuk fields, moving crude entirely by pipeline from northern Iraq to Turkey's Mediterranean export terminal at Ceyhan. Because it bypasses seaborne chokepoints entirely, it gives northern Iraqi and Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) crude a maritime-risk-free route to world markets -- but that same reliance on a single cross-border pipeline makes it uniquely exposed to legal and political disputes between Baghdad, Ankara, and the KRG, as its multi-year shutdown demonstrated.
historical_precedents: Turkey halted flows through the pipeline in March 2023 after an International Chamber of Commerce arbitration ruling in Federal Iraq's favor found that Turkey had improperly allowed the Kurdistan Regional Government to export crude through the pipeline without Federal Iraq's authorization, and ordered Turkey to pay damages. The pipeline then remained shut for roughly two and a half years -- with Iraq's parliament passing a February 2025 budget amendment raising payment rates to independent oil companies to $16 per barrel amid a continued standstill in KRG-Federal Iraq-IOC negotiations as of mid-2025 -- before resuming operations in September 2025.
paths.estimated_global_share: Prior to its March 2023 closure, the Iraq-Turkey Pipeline carried more than 400,000 barrels per day of crude oil exports from northern Iraq to the Ceyhan terminal, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration's Iraq Country Analysis Brief. The pipeline resumed operations in September 2025 after being out of service for about two and a half years, per EIA's World Oil Transit Chokepoints page; EIA has not yet published updated post-reopening throughput figures.

paths.name: East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP): Uganda to Tanzania
origin_regions: Uganda (Lake Albert oil fields, Hoima district)
chokepoints: East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP)
destination_regions: Tanzania (Chongoleani Peninsula marine export terminal near Port of Tanga)
onward seaborne export to global markets
paths.why_it_matters: EACOP is being built as the export route for crude oil from Uganda's landlocked Lake Albert oil fields, running roughly 1,443 kilometers overland from Kabaale in Uganda's Hoima district to a new marine export terminal on the Chongoleani Peninsula near Tanzania's Port of Tanga. Because Uganda has no coastline, the pipeline is effectively the only planned route to bring its crude to world markets at commercial scale, making the project central to whether and when Uganda's oil reserves are monetized; it represents roughly $4 billion of inward investment across the two countries and is backed by TotalEnergies, China's CNOOC, and the Ugandan and Tanzanian national oil companies (UNOC and TPDC).
historical_precedents: Physical construction of the pipeline began in 2024 and was expected to take about two years, after which the project enters a planned roughly 20-year operational phase, per the EACOP project consortium. The World Bank's Uganda country page states Uganda plans to begin exporting crude oil toward the end of 2026 in partnership with TotalEnergies and CNOOC, illustrating the long lead time between a landlocked country's oil discovery and its first commercial export.
paths.estimated_global_share: EACOP has not yet entered commercial operation. Per the World Bank, Uganda plans to begin exporting crude oil toward the end of 2026, and the World Bank's June 2026 Public Finance Review projects oil revenues will begin flowing to the Ugandan government from 2027, averaging roughly 2.2% of GDP per year once exports are underway. The pipeline itself represents about $4 billion of the project's total inward investment across Uganda and Tanzania, per the World Bank and the EACOP project consortium.

paths.name: Mexico and Peru Silver Mine Production for Electronics and Solar
origin_regions: Mexico (Zacatecas, Chihuahua, and Durango mining belts)
chokepoints: Concentration of world silver mine output in a small number of Latin American polymetallic mining districts
Silver is mostly recovered as a byproduct of lead-zinc, copper, and gold mining, so its supply responds slowly to silver-specific price signals
A persistent global supply deficit, with world mine production running well below total consumption from electronics, solar, and investment demand
destination_regions: China, Japan, South Korea, Europe, and the United States (electronics, photovoltaic-cell, and refining industries)
paths.why_it_matters: Silver is a critical input for electrical and electronic contacts, brazing and soldering, and increasingly the conductive paste used in photovoltaic solar cells, alongside its traditional roles in investment bars, coins, and jewelry. Because most of the world's silver is recovered as a byproduct of lead-zinc, copper, and gold mining rather than mined for its own sake, primary supply responds slowly even as industrial and investment demand has outpaced mine output for several consecutive years. Mexico and Peru together account for well over a third of global mine supply, making Latin American polymetallic mining districts the effective anchor of the world's silver pipeline. In November 2025, the U.S. Geological Survey added silver to the U.S. critical minerals list for the first time, formally recognizing its shift from a primarily investment and jewelry metal toward a strategic industrial material used in electronics, solar, and grid technology.
historical_precedents: On November 7, 2025, the U.S. Final 2025 List of Critical Minerals was published in the Federal Register (90 FR 50494), adding silver alongside copper, lead, potash, rhenium, and silicon for the first time; USGS attributed the change to an updated methodology and growing recognition of silver's industrial-demand and supply-concentration risk profile.

Driven by a persistent global supply deficit (2025 world mine production of about 26,000 metric tons against roughly 35,700 metric tons of global consumption, per USGS) and its new critical-mineral status, silver prices climbed to a record intraday high of nearly $122 per troy ounce in late January 2026 -- up roughly fourfold from a year earlier -- before plunging by more than a quarter within days as the rally abruptly reversed.
paths.estimated_global_share: Mexico and Peru together accounted for an estimated 38% of world silver mine production in 2025 (Mexico about 6,300 metric tons and Peru about 3,600 metric tons of 26,000 metric tons world total; Mexico about 24%, Peru about 14%), per the U.S. Geological Survey

paths.name: Venezuela Crude Oil Exports Under U.S. Sanctions Licensing
origin_regions: Venezuela (Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo basin)
chokepoints: U.S. Treasury OFAC sanctions licensing regime governing PDVSA-linked crude exports (chiefly Chevron's general license)
paths.why_it_matters: Unlike the strait and pipeline chokepoints elsewhere in this dataset, the flow of Venezuelan crude to market is gated almost entirely by a small number of U.S. government sanctions licenses rather than by geography. Chevron has for years been the only U.S. major authorized to operate in Venezuela and lift its crude, so a single OFAC licensing decision -- tightening or loosening the terms under which Chevron and, more recently, additional authorized trading companies may export -- can swing measured U.S. imports from near zero to several hundred thousand barrels per day within a matter of months, a volatility pattern with no physical-infrastructure counterpart among the other entries in this dataset.
historical_precedents: OFAC authorized Chevron to resume limited operations in Venezuela in November 2022, and lifted most other U.S. sanctions on Venezuela's energy sector for a six-month window starting October 18, 2023; EIA reported Chevron's share of Venezuelan output rising to about 135,000 barrels per day in 2023 as a result.

U.S. monthly crude oil imports from Venezuela, tracked by EIA, fell from about 300,000 barrels per day in January 2025 to just 6,000 barrels per day in July 2025 after Washington tightened restrictions on Chevron's license (cutting its exports from roughly 250,000 b/d earlier in 2025 to about 100,000 b/d by December 2025, per Pipeline & Gas Journal), before recovering as license terms were expanded to additional authorized trading companies; EIA's weekly data show U.S. imports climbing back into the 400,000-690,000 barrel-per-day range by mid-to-late July 2026.
paths.estimated_global_share: U.S. imports of Venezuelan crude oil -- nearly all of it licensed exports run through Chevron and, since early 2026, additional OFAC-authorized trading companies -- bottomed at about 6,000 barrels per day in July 2025 and rebounded to a weekly average of 673,000 barrels per day for the week ending July 24, 2026, per U.S. Energy Information Administration data.
